No randomized trial has yet tested care guided by the score, so the authors keep it as one voice inside a multimodal assessment that includes lung ultrasound, biomarkers, and clinical response.
pmc-13415428:
Sajawal Abbas Baloch and Aysha Zafar derive exact wave solutions for a nonlinear equation modeling blood vessel behavior, in 2026. The Murray equation here allows vessel wall properties to vary along the vessel. Using transformations and a bilinear approach, they generate many solution families.

Solutions include lump waves, lumps riding with one or two kinks, breathers, periodic waves, and rogue waves. Each pattern maps to a vessel story: lumps mimic local pressure pulses, while rogue waves mimic sudden extreme pressure spikes. Graphs in two and three dimensions show how parameters change wave height and travel. The authors claim this solution range is new for the equation.
pmc-13415528:
Wenqin Huang and co-authors introduce a chip based hollow waveguide whose walls are mostly open air, in 2026. Hollow cores let light interact strongly with gases and liquids, yet sealed walls block molecules from drifting in. Their scaffold design reaches eighty percent openness in the cladding while keeping light losses near those of closed guides.

Guidance mixes anti-resonant confinement with Bloch modes in a segmented membrane, printed in 3D at nanoscale precision. Tests confirmed the principle and loss behavior against a resonator based model. Open walls sped molecular diffusion into the core for sensing. Single photons also passed efficiently, suiting quantum photonics and fluid analysis on one chip.
pmc-13415628:
Toby Falodun, John Masterson, and Nazir I. Lone track how often critical care survivors move between hospital wards, in a 2026 Scottish cohort study. Records covered 12,836 patients admitted through emergency departments at three hospitals between 2017 and 2022, each with a critical care stay before discharge.

Age, illness burden, smoking, deprivation, and organ support level each tracked with how often patients moved. More moves meant higher odds of returning to the emergency department within seven days and a longer hospital stay. Readmission within thirty days and death within thirty days showed no such link. Frequent moves may flag complex patients who need closer early follow-up.
pmc-13416028:
P. Florio and colleagues map which city districts worldwide hold buildings least ready for their climate, in a 2026 global assessment. Building age and compactness stand in for energy efficiency, since old, poorly shaped buildings waste heating or cooling. Stock data and satellite observations were merged across the planet.

About 43 percent of buildings predate 1980, when efficiency rules barely existed, concentrated in temperate and cold cities of rich countries. Vulnerable zones currently house forty-eight million people. Under likely futures that population could grow ten to thirty percent by 2100, shifting toward the Sahel, Gulf states, and Pakistan. Light recent building in poorer countries raises their heat risk.
pmc-13416228:
Rúnarsdóttir and colleagues run a double blind trial in Iceland. It asks what a shellfish derived supplement, chitosan, adds to a lifestyle program for women with obesity. Chitosan is sold as a fat binder, but proof is thin. Their 2026 study randomizes thirty three women to three grams a day of chitosan or placebo for twelve weeks, inside a rehabilitation program. It tracks body makeup by DXA, strength, blood pressure, and gut microbes from stool.

The lifestyle program did the heavy lifting: grip strength, endurance, lean mass, and self rated health all rose, while body fat and blood pressure fell, in both arms. Chitosan's fingerprint was microbial, lowering the ratio between two bacteria groups without singling out any one species. Women with the highest body mass index lost microbe diversity regardless of arm. With thirty three participants, the authors frame the microbe shifts as leads for trials, not verdicts.
pmc-13417728:
The EFSA GMO Panel assesses a stacked modified soybean in a 2026 opinion for the European Food Safety Authority. The soybean joins two past events so plants can survive four herbicide types. Each event had passed past panel reviews with no safety concerns. New data on the single events raised no fresh issues.

Checks of the plant's make up, field traits, and food value found no new concerns from the stack. Tests for harm, allergy, and nutrition were also clear. The panel judges the soybean as safe as standard types for food and feed. No post market food checks are needed, and spilled seed raises no green concerns.
pmc-13418128:
Dukhyun Back, Kihye Han, and Hyang Baek sort South Korean hospital nurses into climate behaviour profiles, in a 2026 survey study. Nurses are the largest health workforce, and hospitals emit heavily, so their habits matter. Survey data from 861 nurses fed a latent profile analysis based on eight behaviour items covering daily mitigation actions.

Three profiles emerged: low engagement at about 9 percent, moderate at 45 percent, and high at 46 percent. Driving less separated low from moderate groups most. High engagers reported more extreme weather experience and stronger confidence, individually and collectively. Oddly, more climate information exposure linked to lower engagement, while short staffing blocked greener habits.
pmc-13418728:
Sarra K Mohamed Ahmed and colleagues describe an 87-year-old woman whose thyroid failure reached a life-threatening stage even though her blood tests looked only mildly off. She carried long-term hypothyroidism, adrenal failure, pituitary disease, and heart disease into the hospital with a urinary infection. Her body temperature, pulse, and blood pressure all fell, her awareness faded, and her gut slowed despite standard antibiotic care.

Her thyroid tests showed a mildly raised stimulating hormone with a near-normal thyroxine level, which could have misled the team. Slow-relaxing ankle reflexes on a repeat exam pointed the other way, and a standard scoring system gave strong support for the severe diagnosis. Care shifted to steroid and thyroid hormone drips, active warming, and close support, and she recovered well. The case warns clinicians to trust the full clinical picture over mild lab values.
pmc-13419228:
Elizabeth A. McHuron and colleagues build formulas for the daily energy cost of milk production in marine mammals, where direct measures are rare or missing. Energy budgets help scientists judge how disturbance, like noise or lost feeding time, may hit seal and whale populations. Milk feeding is one of the largest costs a mother pays, so getting it right matters for the whole budget.

The team derived links from the species where milk intake and energy density have been measured. Fully water-living whales may break the pattern set by seals, a caveat the authors flag for care. Checks against fresh estimates supported the formulas for seals, sea lions, and marine mustelids, with stated limits. Wildlife managers can now fill a key gap for species that have never been measured directly.
pmc-13420128:
Lloyd-Bradley and Hattersley reviewed records for 18 cats fitted with a subcutaneous ureteral bypass device, an implanted tube system that reroutes urine around a blocked ureter, between 2016 and 2022. Their referral-center study asked how often blood appears in the urine after this surgery, a finding whose importance for the cats was unclear.

All 18 cats developed microscopic blood in the urine after surgery, first detected at a median of one month and usually on the very first urine check. Fourteen cats, or 78 percent, had persistent findings, and severe blood levels appeared in 13 cats at some point. Visible bloody urine was rare, reported in only 2 of the 18 cats overall. In 11 cats the blood appeared without any positive urine culture, and the authors call for work on its cause and significance.
pmc-13420328:
Marion Caumeil and co-authors present a case showing how blood-based monitoring can expose drug resistance in lung cancer before scans do. Their 2026 report follows a woman aged 66 whose lung cancer carried the KRAS G12C mutation treated with adagrasib, a drug targeting that mutation, after chemotherapy and immunotherapy failed.

Tumour DNA in her blood fell sharply after seven weeks, showing an initial response, then rose at months four and six. Sequencing revealed three new KRAS mutations alongside the original one, a pattern called polyclonal resistance, where several resistant cell groups grow at once. Her scans stayed stable by standard criteria throughout this period. Significant clinical decline followed about eight weeks after the first DNA rise, and she died two months after the resistance mutations were found. The authors argue serial liquid biopsies can flag resistance early.
pmc-13421428:
Ulziijargal Bayarsaikhan and five colleagues record, in a 2026 paper, the moth tribe Artonini in Korea for the first time in organised form. These small day-flying moths belong to the burnet moth family, and the Korean fauna of this tribe had not been reviewed as a group.

Five species in two genera are documented. One, Amuria baei, is described as new to science. The paper illustrates adults and their genitalia — the structures taxonomists rely on to separate close species — for every recorded member of the tribe. It closes with a checklist of all zygaenid moths known from Korea, arranged under a 2024 classification. The work gives Korean entomology a reference point for this group.
pmc-13422828:
Kwesiga and co-authors compare two ways of reaching depressed young people in Kampala, Uganda, in this 2026 qualitative study. One is tele-support psychotherapy delivered by phone with lay counselors. The other is standard in-person mental health services. Interviews and focus groups with youth aged 15 to 30 and with counselors were analyzed against an implementation science framework.

The backdrop is stark engagement data from the parent trial, where 61.69 percent of youth assigned to phone therapy actually engaged, against just 10.27 percent for in-person services in the figures reported. Phone delivery won on cost, travel, and flexible scheduling, and counselors' rapport skills helped, but unreliable mobile connectivity undermined it. In-person care suffered from high costs and low public awareness. Social support and higher income eased participation in both arms, and the authors call for fixing connectivity and literacy gaps.
pmc-13422928:
Cascio and a large team collect stories rather than scores in this 2026 Italian narrative medicine project, named DIAMOND, spanning 19 centers. Patients with chronic pain, epilepsy, serious Gram-positive infections, or depression wrote illness stories. So did the people who cared for them. Treating doctors kept matching charts, recording the same visits from their side.

The project took in stories from 64 patients and 56 family carers, plus 40 charts from 20 doctors. Pain came up in the stories as an embodied weight. It was shown through metaphors of darkness and distortion. Fear and shock at diagnosis sometimes grew into acceptance. Family carers spoke of heavy burdens and frequent helplessness. Doctors' charts ran more technical and forward-looking, showing a perceptual gap about what illness means. Most people found the writing itself helpful. The authors argue such story methods surface unmet needs that checklists miss.
pmc-13423828:
Sarah Brunner heads a 36-author mouse study showing that gut microbes actively limit how much dietary fat the intestine absorbs. Using isotope-labelled fats in germ-free and colonised mice, the team modelled whole-body lipid handling. Colonised animals kept far more fat in the gut. Their intestinal contents held up to twelve times more lipid than those of germ-free mice.

Protein and lipid profiling traced the chain: microbes trigger a host signalling pathway that lifts production of the bile salt taurocholate. That salt switches on a fat-splitting enzyme in bile, which destroys phosphatidylcholine, a molecule needed to package fat for uptake. Richer microbial communities meant less of that packaging lipid, and so less absorption.
pmc-13424028:
Tkachenko and colleagues mapped in 2026 how the sheep lung develops, cell by cell, in health and in cystic fibrosis. Sheep lungs resemble human lungs, and sheep let researchers study late pregnancy stages that cannot be studied in people. The team read gene activity in single cells from upper and lower lung at three points from mid pregnancy to birth. They studied normal sheep and sheep engineered to lack a working CFTR gene.

Tkachenko traced changes in cell identity and counts that show how support, vessel, and lining cells mature over time. Sheep without CFTR, the gene whose loss causes cystic fibrosis, already showed distinct cell signatures in the lung before birth. Those early signatures may help explain features of the disease seen soon after birth in babies. The atlas gives a baseline for judging lung development and early disease shifts.
pmc-13424128:
Weijia Fu and six colleagues use genetics to find genes whose activity in the prostate predicts how long men survive prostate cancer. Linking inherited predictors of gene expression with survival data from a Swedish cohort, then checking a large American trial cohort, they scanned across tissues: healthy prostate, primary tumours, and metastatic tumours.

Seven genes at one spot on chromosome 1 passed both discovery and validation. Higher activity of RCC1 tracked with faster return of a blood marker signalling relapse, while higher PHACTR4 appeared in tumours of worse grade. The authors note the work covers European ancestry only and shows association, not cause, so wider populations and lab tests must follow.
pmc-13424428:
Reid Weisberg and seven colleagues teach a large language model to pull a standard arthritis activity score out of free-text clinic notes, where such scores usually hide. The Clinical Disease Activity Index guides rheumatoid arthritis care, and the team worked in a warehouse holding records for over 4.5 million patients at a New York academic centre.

Among 2,756 patients with arthritis notes, the index or its parts could be extracted for a minority, 15.4% of the antibody-positive group showing documented remission or low activity among them. Documentation ran richer for patients with many notes and for faculty authors. Against expert chart review the automated extraction scored 0.97 on precision, recall, and combined measure, a first for this zero-shot approach.
pmc-13424728:
Aisling McCarthy leads an eleven-author analysis of gender differences in low blood sugar among people with type 1 or insulin-treated type 2 diabetes, from the ten-week Hypo-METRICS study. Nearly six hundred participants took part: 321 with type 2 diabetes and 274 with type 1. All wore blinded glucose sensors and logged symptoms in real time through a dedicated phone app.

Time spent in low glucose did not differ between women and men in either group. Experience told another story: women reported more symptomatic episodes per week than men, even though the sensors saw equal exposure. Autonomic symptoms such as hunger and shaking and brain-fog symptoms such as confusion were catalogued separately. The authors stress that counting sensor lows alone understates the lived burden for women.
pmc-13425528:
Shanshan Liu, Lu Liu, and Jian Dong evaluated blood biomarkers for early heart injury in severe community-acquired pneumonia in a 2026 prospective cohort study. Heart injury in such patients is often missed, and troponin readings can be muddied by kidney problems and critical illness. The team tested admission interleukin-8 and soluble ST2, alone and combined, in 146 patients.

Injury was defined by high-sensitivity troponin I above the assay cutoff, and receiver operating curve analysis with cross-validation judged how well each marker flagged cases. Kidney-function-stratified troponin thresholds were also explored, offering readers candidate tools for earlier risk sorting in severe pneumonia.
pmc-13425828: Shaosen Zhang and coauthors issued a correction concerning their protocol for growing organoids from normal and cancer-prone human esophageal tissue. During manuscript preparation, a duplicated portion of the high-grade lesion image was mistakenly placed over the low-grade image in the floating organoids row of Figure 1D. The notice supplies the corrected panel and states that the error does not change the conclusions of the figure or the protocol, with an apology for any inconvenience. The notice is a correction only and carries no new experimental content.
pmc-13426028:
Katherine Brittain and colleagues used DNA evidence to test whether the tiny freshwater crocodiles of rocky uplands in northern Australia form a separate species. These pygmy crocodiles mature earlier and reach only about half the adult size of downstream crocodiles.

The team read two stretches of DNA passed down from mothers, plus thousands of markers from across the genome. Pygmy and normal crocodiles shared the same DNA types, and grouping followed place more than body size. No clear genetic line split the pygmy form off as its own species, though each upland group still differed somewhat. Brittain argues the pygmy crocodiles still merit strong protection as distinct, isolated populations facing invaders and climate change.
pmc-13426228:
Tom N. Durrant and coauthors define a feedback loop between Rac and PI3K-beta in platelet activation in a 2026 study. Knockin mice carrying two mutations in the Rho-binding domain of the enzyme's catalytic subunit showed impaired GPVI signaling, function, and spreading on fibrinogen.

A selective PI3K-beta inhibitor reproduced most defects, and blocking Rac or Cdc42 in normal platelets copied the knockin pattern. The loop helps explain how platelets build stable clots under high shear flow.
pmc-13426428:
Ward Vleeshouwers and colleagues show that the time of day when the immune system first meets a germ shapes the memory cells it keeps. Memory CD8 T cells are the long-lived defenders that respond fast when a virus returns.

Vaccination during the active phase of the day produced more early-stage memory cells and stronger protection against later virus challenge. Those cells carry their own body clocks, which timed how much of a helper signal called CD70 they showed. Vleeshouwers suggests timing vaccines to the body clock could sharpen lasting immunity.
pmc-13427428:
Jacob B. O'Brien and colleagues measured return to sport after reverse shoulder replacement in an active Australian cohort in a 2026 retrospective single-surgeon study. Reverse arthroplasty is increasingly offered to younger, active patients with shoulder arthritis or rotator cuff arthropathy, yet sport outcomes were rarely reported. The series covered 152 physically active patients operated between January 2020 and January 2024 with one implant system.

Twelve-month outcomes captured return rate, timing, performance level, pain, and satisfaction with function, with regression hunting predictors of success. Patients weighing this operation gain realistic timelines for resuming sport. One skilled pair of hands did each case, which keeps skill gaps from cloud the tale, though it may not match less deft hands in small towns.
pmc-13427628:
Bingya Zhang and Yihang Gao review, in 2026, cancer drug carriers modeled on exosomes, the tiny parcels cells naturally use to pass material between them. Standard cancer drugs spread through the whole body, causing harm while often reaching tumors poorly. Exosomes slip past many body barriers and are well tolerated, which makes them attractive delivery vehicles. The review covers natural exosomes, altered ones, hybrids, and lab-made mimics.

These carriers can haul chemotherapy drugs, gene material, and immune treatments, and some combine therapy with imaging. Production remains the hard part: yields are low, loads vary, and quality is hard to standardize. Safety testing and approval rules also lag behind the science. Readers weighing this field get both the promise and the manufacturing reality in one place.
pmc-13427928:

Gene variants make people fast or slow processors, with real dosing effects. An expert panel from a global pharmacogenetics group reviewed the evidence allele by allele.

The panel assigned plain clinical labels to 59 known variants of the gene. Two variants earned the increased-function label, the fast-processing kind. Forty variants were classed as decreased function, the slow-processing kind. Ten stayed uncertain and seven unknown for lack of solid evidence. pmc-13428428:
Zhang and colleagues asked whether body composition predicts sleep disturbance in American adults, using the ratio of skeletal muscle mass to visceral fat as a combined marker of sarcopenic obesity. The highest ratio quartile showed 57.4 percent lower risk than the lowest, with a clear linear dose-response pattern across quartiles. Inflammation and accelerated biological aging partly explained the link, mediating 10.64 percent through one composite index, 36.43 percent through another, and 15.99 percent through phenotypic age acceleration.
pmc-13428728:
Oliver M. Schleicher and co-authors study how often high-grade cervical cell changes disappear without treatment in young women. Their 2026 retrospective study follows women aged 30 or younger who were managed by observation at a certified dysplasia unit in Erlangen between 2014 and 2025.

The cohort held 45 patients with the more severe CIN3 changes and 38 with CIN2 changes. Regression occurred in 46.7 percent of the CIN3 group and 63.2 percent of the CIN2 group, most of it within the first year of follow-up. Regression was linked to clearance of human papillomavirus in both groups, and no patient progressed to invasive cancer. The authors suggest virus clearance, HPV16 status, and vaccination history could help select patients for watchful management.
pmc-13429128:

Toric lenses implanted at cataract surgery cancel astigmatism, and surgeons sometimes aim for slight overcorrection that flips the remaining error to the opposite axis. Vision and refraction matched between groups on every standard measure. Most fine distortions also matched, with one exception: a distortion pattern called trefoil measured higher in the flipped group. Adjusted analysis confirmed the flip itself tracked with that single distortion. No other outcome moved with it. Patients can be told that a planned flip costs nothing in ordinary vision terms, based on these results.
pmc-13430528:
Gerardo Arreola Jardón and colleagues made thin films of zinc telluride mixed with copper and oxygen, aiming at better parts for solar cells. They used a spraying method called radio-frequency sputtering, firing material from a single mixed target onto heated surfaces.

Copper and oxygen levels ran from 3 to 13 percent of atoms, and films grew at two heat settings. Tests showed all films held two crystal forms of zinc telluride, and richer mixes grew a second, copper-rich phase. That phase cut infrared light passing through the films and made them conduct far better, with resistance dropping by about ten thousand times. Arreola Jardón links these traits to back-contact layers, the metal-facing parts of cadmium telluride solar cells.
pmc-13430828:
Carlo Fiore and colleagues tracked the nerve fiber layer at the back of the eye after four types of glaucoma surgery. Glaucoma means a group of eye diseases that slowly kill the nerve cells carrying vision to the brain.

The team reviewed 462 eyes treated with four different operations or drainage devices, following scans for two years. Eye pressure and the number of pressure-lowering drugs fell in every group, and eyesight stayed stable. Yet the nerve fiber layer kept thinning during the first year after surgery in all four groups. No clear further thinning showed in the second year, so Fiore advises watching this layer closely after any glaucoma operation.
pmc-13431028:
Disantis and colleagues set the score changes that count as success for young people with acetabular dysplasia, a shallow hip socket, who choose physiotherapy over surgery. Scores alone mean little without a bar for what patients feel. Their 2026 study follows 45 patients aged 10 to 35 at two centers through eight to ten weeks of therapy. It uses a twelve item hip questionnaire plus anchor questions on satisfaction and function.

Just over half the patients landed in the improved group. The smallest change patients can feel, the minimal clinically important difference, came out at eight and a half points. A change of about fifteen points marked the state patients call acceptable, and a score of 62 separated satisfied from unsatisfied patients with good accuracy. A maximal outcome improvement bar, near a quarter above baseline, was also set. Clinicians can now judge therapy against what patients themselves call enough.
pmc-13431228:
Finna E Indriany and a large team piloted a phone-based home watch system for heart failure patients in Indonesia in 2026, mixing build work with a small trial of effects. Home self-checks aim to cut fresh hospital stays and lift daily life for such patients. Sixty patients joined, split evenly between the new system and standard care.

Fresh stays struck a fifth of the watch group and well over two fifths of the standard group, a gap the small trial could not confirm with firm proof. Scores on a heart health survey rose more in the watch group across most areas, from body limits to daily quality. Deaths ran lower in the watch group as well. The authors call the setup workable and ask for larger trials to settle its worth.
pmc-13431428:

It found one lower pain score and less rescue pain drug use in the first day for the added-agent group.

That gap matters, since the lone time point with a group gap is the one in doubt. The letter also faults loose repeat testing with no set main time point. A fuller model of pain over time would give a sounder read, the writers argue.
pmc-13433128:
Kowal and colleagues check for chemical tags on mitochondrial DNA in dog mammary tumors in this preliminary 2026 study. Two of the three sequence contexts examined, called CpG and CHH, varied more between tumor and normal tissue than the third, CHG, which stayed comparatively stable throughout. Differences in the two variable contexts moved together with a strong correlation in this small sample, suggesting coordinated change in tumors. The authors stress the group of six dogs is too small for conclusions and frame the work as a first indication worth testing at scale.
pmc-13433428:

Scans found plaque in twenty-nine patients across three grades. The new tracing caught all but one case, a catch rate near total, while the plain tracing caught two. Grade by grade, the new tool hit full marks at the low and high ends. The authors pitch it as a sorting gate before scans or specialist trips, with larger multi-center trials still owed.
pmc-13434128:
Jessica J King and coauthors present a 2026 method for mapping where cells sit inside lab grown balls of cells and how those cells respond to drugs. DNA tags mark each cell by its place in the ball. The team builds the balls layer by layer and then reads gene activity cell by cell.

Tests with HeLa cell balls show that cells in one place do not all react to a drug in the same way. The authors link the uneven response to how far a drug can spread, plus gaps in food, energy use, and cell stress. Readers gain a clear route to richer drug screens that keep place and gene activity together.
pmc-13434928:
Critén and colleagues followed Swedish older adults for twenty-three years in 2026 to test whether serious gum disease at the start predicted death from any cause. Gum disease has been tied to heart disease and diabetes, but long-run evidence on death risk is thinner. The study drew on a national aging project in Karlskrona. Dental and X-ray exams covered 340 people who entered in their early sixties, back in 2001 to 2003, and were followed from there.

About one in six participants had moderate-to-severe gum disease at baseline, and just over half of that group died during follow-up. After adjusting for age, sex, smoking, and other factors, the gum disease group carried about a one-and-a-half-fold higher risk of death. The authors note the link sits at the edge of statistical certainty.
pmc-13436428:
Rafael M Batista and coauthors test whether telling people the cost of holding savings beside card debt changes behavior in 2026. Banking records over thirty eight months show co holding in twenty three percent of card users. A field trial then messaged 125,328 customers through their bank app.

Messages spelled out the waste and offered one tap transfers to pay debt. Repayment amounts did not move in any real way. Customers did repay more often and paid above minimums more. Habit and mental buckets, not ignorance, seem to hold the pattern. Banks may need stronger tools than clear information.
pmc-13437428:

Guidelines push sacubitril/valsartan to a top dose, yet many patients stall lower over side effects. Their 2026 study built a body-based simulator of how the drug moves and acts, checked it against real patient data, and extended it to kidney and heart failure groups.

The simulator matched real drug levels closely, with nearly nine in ten predictions landing near measured values. When the team linked those levels to a heart strain marker, raising the dose from half to full added little extra benefit. The same step deepened blood pressure drops and the tolerance worries that come with them. They offer the model as early support for holding at the lower dose.
pmc-13437528:
Katarzyna Lisowicz and colleagues measured work stress among nurses and hunted for the factors that push it up. Their 2026 survey covered 588 nurses in three hospitals, using a standard work appraisal questionnaire plus the team's own questions.

Stress ran high across the group. It peaked in nurses working overtime and in those caring for many patients at once. Intensive care units recorded the highest levels, while primary care posts recorded the lowest. In the combined model, older age and being female raised stress, while longer service lowered it; education, shift system, and overtime each played a part. The authors read stress as a many-sided problem in which workplace design weighs at least as much as personal traits. Cutting ratios and overtime, they argue, is the most direct lever.
pmc-13438128:
Mahalingam and colleagues study how alcohol distorts the hunger hormone ghrelin in this 2026 cell study. Ghrelin, made in the stomach, normally rises during fasting, but chronic drinking raises it further, fueling craving and worsening liver disease. The cellular mechanism was unknown, so the team exposed ghrelin-producing stomach and pancreatic cell lines to alcohol for 48 hours and measured hormone production and energy metabolism.

Alcohol increased ghrelin secretion and switched on the genes for ghrelin and for the enzyme that activates it. Normally, high glucose suppresses ghrelin release, but alcohol pretreatment blunted that brake, so cells behaved as if starving amid plenty. Alcohol also raised glucose uptake while cutting the cells' sugar-burning capacity. It profoundly reduced three rate-limiting glycolytic enzymes. The authors propose that combination as a therapeutic target.
pmc-13439028:
Alfina Nur Isyrofi and colleagues offer a 2026 review that compares three food fibres and their effects on metabolism. The fibres are oat beta-glucan, rice bran, and flour made from unripe bananas. Each works in a distinct way, through thickness in the gut, plant compounds that affect fats, or starch that feeds gut microbes. Past trials mostly tested one fibre at a time, often with few people and short follow-up.

Following the PRISMA 2020 rules for reviews, the authors gather human studies on blood sugar, blood fats, and blood pressure. They weigh dose, food form, and how each fibre acts in the body. Readers get a side-by-side account meant to guide food choices for people at risk of metabolic syndrome, a cluster of weight, sugar, and pressure problems.
pmc-13439128:
Douglas A Corley and colleagues study a large integrated care model in the United States and its links to death rates and lifespan, in work published in 2026. The model joins many proven population health steps across diseases in one system. Few data showed what happens when such steps run together at scale. The team compared members with several other groups, including national figures and people with like insurance and health profiles.

Nearly four million people were followed in the analysis. Adjusted death rates ran lower for nine of ten leading causes, counting cancer, heart disease, stroke, injury, and lung disease. Members lived notably longer than the national average in 2023, with the largest gains in the 50 to 72 age range. Gaps between demographic groups also ran smaller than in the comparison groups.
pmc-13439228:
Yingxiu Wang, Sizhe Xu, Jingzhu Guo, and Timothy Noel Stephens survey sleep among hospital staff in Haikou, China, just after the COVID pandemic, in a 2026 study. Poor sleep harms health workers and patient safety alike, yet post-pandemic drivers were unclear. In April 2023 the team invited clinical staff at one large hospital to answer a 33-item survey. Replies came from 525 staff and covered sleep quality, anxiety, and low mood with standard short scales.

Over half the staff scored in the poor sleep range. Nurses slept worse than doctors and other clinical staff, while staff with more schooling slept better. Night shifts, anxiety, and low mood each linked to worse sleep on their own. The authors urge hospitals to spot staff at risk early and to test ways of guarding sleep in shift-based care.
pmc-13439528:
David M Whalley and co-authors unveil a fast, single route to glutarimide building blocks prized in protein-degrader drugs, reporting in 2026. Glutarimides anchor medicines that hijack cereblon, a cell protein that tags other proteins for disposal. Drugs from thalidomide kin to newer degraders rely on the motif, yet older syntheses took many steps and slowed testing of new variants. Their platform starts from common nitrogen ring compounds and runs three steps in sequence.

A phosphine-catalysed bond formation, a metal-free radical addition, and an acid-driven ring closing deliver varied glutarimides with high selectivity. The route tolerates many chemical groups and scales from grams to rapid parallel batches. With it, the team built cereblon binder libraries, control analogues, and late-stage tweaks of active molecules. The authors pitch the platform as a way to speed degrader discovery.
pmc-13439928: Bouillon and colleagues published a correction in 2026. It amends their paper on genes and fruit traits in cider apples, in the journal G3. The note is a correction, and it fixes two short parts of the methods. One part now states the cut-off used to call a gene link real. The other part now gives the right first line on how mean fruit traits were worked out by year.
pmc-13441228:
Yang and colleagues reported in 2026 a case of acute aortic dissection that unfolded without the sudden severe pain the condition is famous for. The condition is a tear in the wall of the body's main artery. The patient was a 55-year-old woman brought in with weakness, agitation, and breathlessness. A painless start is uncommon and dangerous, because teams may look elsewhere while the tear spreads.

A first bedside ultrasound looked reassuring, but the woman stayed agitated and developed belly tenderness. A repeat ultrasound then showed signs of dissection, and a CT scan confirmed a tear in the rising aorta, the most lethal type. Despite intense resuscitation, her condition collapsed quickly and she could not be saved. The authors urge repeat scanning whenever symptoms shift in ways that do not fit the first picture.
pmc-13441328:
Lucas Cruz and colleagues survey how music is chosen and used inside psychedelic-assisted psychotherapy trials, publishing a 2026 systematic review. Music shapes psychedelic sessions in clinic and recreational settings alike, and may sway outcomes. Searches across five databases under standard review rules found thirty-six articles, of which twenty-five described music use. Most work targeted depression and post-traumatic stress, using psilocybin or MDMA as the drug partner.

Playlist building varied widely between studies, from fixed canonical lists to personalised sets, with little shared protocol. Differences in disorder and substance explained part of the spread, though reporting habits explained plenty more. Few papers described who chose tracks, when music changed across a session, or how volume and genre were set. The authors argue that naming which musical choices get privileged would let future trials test music as a treatment ingredient rather than set dressing.
pmc-13442528:
Addison Kitrel and colleagues probe how loneliness ties to low mood in older adults with cancer in a 2026 study. The group held 258 people aged 70 years or more who had joined a talk-therapy trial for distress. Each person rated social isolation, mood, worry, views on aging, and a sense of lost meaning at the trial start.

Isolation scores rose hand in hand with low mood scores on two mood scales, with strong links in the raw checks. Full models that weighed age, sex, and other traits still tied isolation to low mood on its own. Worry and lost meaning also held solo links to low mood. The authors argue that loneliness is not just a shadow of other woes in this group. Clinics that screen for isolation may catch a treatable driver of distress in older cancer care.
pmc-13444128:
Leon French and colleagues test whether two giant mouse brain atlases name the same cell crowds in a 2026 study. Each atlas sorted more than 4 million cells into more than 5,000 clusters, one from whole cells and one from nuclei. Neighbor votes across full gene profiles checked which clusters match both ways.

A total of 2,009 cluster pairs matched in return, with shared map spots and gene tunes, also seen in other species' sets. Cerebellum clusters matched best, since that zone holds less cell variety. The hypothalamus, rich and varied, matched worst. Close twin clusters proved hardest to split, above all by marker genes alone. The authors add match grades so users can weigh atlas claims with care.
pmc-13447428:
Wei Liu and colleagues describe minimally invasive surgery for a spinal blood vessel fault using tube retractors and CT guidance in a 2026 case report with literature review. The fault, an abnormal artery-to-vein link near the spinal cord covering, can damage movement and sensation if missed, and open surgery can weaken the spine. Two patients were treated with the gentler approach.

Scans during surgery pinpointed each fault, and dye imaging confirmed closure on the spot. Both faults were fully closed through the narrow tube, with symptom improvement afterwards and no surgical complications during the hospital stay. Sparing muscle, ligament and bone should speed recovery and protect spinal stability compared with open exposure. Longer follow-up and more cases are still needed before the method can be judged against vessel-blocking treatment from inside.
pmc-13448428:
Starzer and colleagues present in 2026, as abstract CLTR-08, early results from a prospective observational registry of metastatic breast cancer patients with leptomeningeal disease. This is cancer coating the membranes around the brain and spinal cord, a setting with poor prognosis and little data on newer brain-active drugs.

Twenty-eight women had enrolled so far, median age fifty-three at leptomeningeal diagnosis, spanning all breast cancer subtypes. As first treatment, about forty-six percent received radiation, just over half systemic therapy alone. Half the cohort was treated with trastuzumab deruxtecan, a modern antibody-drug conjugate, including nine patients whose tumors counted as HER2-low. Median time on that drug was six months; eight patients had stopped for progression and two for toxicity, while four remained on treatment. Spinal fluid sampling proved workable: of seven patients successfully tested, six carried targetable genomic alterations.
pmc-13448928:
Suji Im and colleagues tackle in 2026 a growth problem for gallium oxide, a semiconductor prized for future power electronics. Its most stable form grows well on its natural cleavage face, yet that face is so flat that arriving atoms find few step edges where they can settle and join the crystal. The team used heat treatment to break the wide flat terraces into narrower strips separated by substeps about half a unit cell high.

On these substep-templated surfaces, crystal growth ran at about 2.83 micrometers per hour, faster than earlier reports for this orientation, while keeping sound structure and working electronic behavior. The authors compare their approach with other tricks for boosting nucleation, such as using higher-energy faces or deliberate miscuts. They conclude that carving substeps into the flat face offers a practical route to better films for advanced devices.
pmc-13449928:
Kirti Saluja, Dipanjan Roy, and Arpan Banerjee trace in 2026 how the brain's echo of each heartbeat changes across the adult lifespan. They recorded brain magnetic activity and heart signals together in 620 adults aged eighteen to eighty-eight, all resting quietly. The heartbeat-evoked response, the cortex's timed reaction to each beat, forms a window on interoception, the sensing of the body's inner state that feeds attention, emotion, and time perception.

That echo weakened systematically with age in the window 180 to 320 milliseconds after each beat. Heart signals did not grow louder overall; instead they reset the phase of theta brain rhythms, and this locking grew more consolidated, not less, in older adults. The response's home also migrated from frontal toward temporal regions with age, and directional analysis showed influence flowing more from heart to brain and less back. The authors read a lifetime reorganization of body-brain dialogue in these shifts.
pmc-13450028:
Longchao Chen and colleagues report in 2026 a late surprise from a kidney cancer type considered too lazy to travel. Eosinophilic solid and cystic renal cell carcinoma, recognized only in 2022 and making up a fifth of one percent of kidney tumors, rarely metastasizes. Their patient, a 57-year-old woman, had her left kidney removed in 2018 for this tumor while her adrenal gland was deliberately spared, since nothing suggested its involvement.

Six years later she returned with a solitary deposit in that same-side adrenal gland, and the cancer had grown as a thrombus into the adrenal and leftover renal veins. The drug pazopanib was stopped. A robotic operation removed the gland and cleared the vein clots in one go. Pathology confirmed metastatic disease of the same type. One year on she remained recurrence-free, evidence the authors offer that late spread of this indolent tumor can reward decisive surgery.
pmc-13451428: The journal Bioscience Reports issued an Expression of Concern in 2026 about a paper by Liang and colleagues. That paper claimed a small RNA protects the lungs in acute respiratory distress syndrome. It was said to act by targeting p65. The journal cites peer-review concerns and duplicated images. Panels closely matched images in a 2020 paper by Wei. The authors supplied raw data, but the originally submitted images were absent. Western blot scans carried a labelling discrepancy. The article stays published, with this permanent notice attached.
pmc-13452128:
Hongping Jia and co-authors review in 2026 tiny RNA snips cut from carrier RNAs as new marks and tools against stomach cancer. Stomach cancer still kills heavily, and today's blood marks miss too much. The snips, called tRFs, are stable in body fluids and steer genes in ways that partly set them apart from their better-known microRNA kin.

Patient samples show tRF patterns that sort cancer with force past older marks, and the review names lead candidates. Yet the same snip can act in opposed ways, lab reads vary, and no trial has yet tested them in care. The authors call for shared lab rules and hard proof before clinics adopt the snips.
pmc-13452228:
Chao Tang and co-authors vet in 2026 a pickle-born lactic germ as a natural guard for pork. Chemical guards raise fears of resistance and residue, so food labs hunt germ-based swaps. The strain, a Pediococcus from Yangzhou pickles, hit three food-poison germs hardest among those tried, and its gene read found no plasmids, no movable drug-proof genes, and no classic harm factors.

Its cell-free brew, at a set strength, held down both native spoilage germs and seeded poison germs on pork through a week in the cold. Meat color, bite feel, and fat rust stayed steady. The team offers the strain as a lead for clean-label meat guards.
pmc-13453028:
Wang and colleagues reported a 2026 study on a new compound against liver cancer. Hepatocellular carcinoma grows fast, spreads early, and often resists standard drugs. The team tested a lab-made compound called KZL-064 on cancer cells and mice. They also hunted for the exact protein the compound locks onto.

The compound slowed cell growth, movement, and invasion in lab tests. It pushed cancer cells into self-destruction and halted their division cycle. In mice, the drug by mouth shrank tumors about as well as a standard drug. Tests showed it binds a protein named HDAC1, which controls gene switching. Blocking that protein explained part, but not all, of the drug effect. More lab work is still needed to pin down the other targets it may hit.
pmc-13453528:
Lucas S Santana and fourteen co-authors search for inherited gene changes in people whose high blood pressure stems from both adrenal glands making too much aldosterone. This hormone disorder, primary aldosteronism, often hides behind hard to control pressure. Their 2026 study covers 53 people with the bilateral form who had resistant pressure or pressure starting before age 40.

Whole exome sequencing, which reads all protein coding genes, found rare candidate changes in 9 of the 53 people. Five sat in genes already tied to the disorder, most often CACNA1H, which helps control a calcium channel. Four more sat in plausible new candidate genes. Carriers needed more pressure drugs and showed more gland changes on scans, yet had low potassium less often. All the changes remain of uncertain weight, the authors note, so more proof is needed.
pmc-13454228:
Yixian Zhu and nine co-authors test whether fading intrinsic capacity, the body's reserve across movement, mind, and senses, warns of later depression and anxiety. Their 2026 study draws 403,018 UK Biobank members recruited from 2006 to 2010, with outcomes tracked over 12.7 years. A deficit score sums faults across seven measures in four capacity domains.

New depression arose in 18,893 people and new anxiety in 22,320 during follow up. Those with the heaviest deficit scores, four or more, faced 3.70 times the depression risk of those with a clean score. Anxiety risk ran 3.01 times higher, and the combined outcome 3.14 times. Later mental health surveys in a subgroup backed the pattern. The authors present low capacity as a useful early flag, while noting that trials must test whether rebuilding capacity prevents illness.
pmc-13454328:
Xiong Zhang and five colleagues report, in 2026, a survey study of how families cope when a member lives with long-term heart failure. The team recruited 536 patients from large hospitals in Yunnan Province, China. Questionnaires covered family coping, tiredness, and how well the family works as a unit.

A grouping method sorted the families into two patterns. About 57 percent showed a constructive pattern, scoring higher on every coping measure. The other 43 percent showed a draining pattern. Families that worked well together, mid-sized families, and higher-income families were less likely to fall into the draining pattern. Small nuclear families were more likely to land there. The authors say support programs should target family habits, not just the patient.
pmc-13454828:
Yunyun Chen and five colleagues build, in a 2026 study, a scoring chart to flag high-risk womb lining cancer before major surgery settles the question. Risk class today depends on what surgeons find after removal, which delays planning. The team studied 130 patients at one Chinese hospital, splitting them into training and check groups.

Stain tests on tumor tissue and routine blood values fed the comparison between high-risk and low-risk cases. Three factors stood on their own: patient age, a growth marker called Ki-67, and the blood ratio of lymphocytes to monocytes. A chart combining the three beat each factor alone at sorting risk in the training group. The check group supported the chart's value. The authors offer the tool for earlier, sharper treatment planning, while noting the small single-hospital sample behind it.
pmc-13455628:
Zhang and colleagues improve an imaging method for monitoring a cancer therapy called electroporation in this 2026 study. Electroporation uses electric pulses to open cell membranes, and electroacoustic tomography images the treated zone from sound waves the pulses generate. In clinics only a single viewing angle is practical, which badly distorts the reconstructed image. The team built a two-stage deep learning model, EXPP-Net, to repair it.

The first stage predicts the missing views from one measured view, and the second polishes the rough reconstruction into a full-view-quality image. Trained on water-tank experiments with rotating electrodes, the model rebuilt images that closely matched full-view scans, reaching structural similarity scores of about 0.997 with the linear probe setup tested. Tests with a second probe type and in a living mouse also showed strong distortion correction.
pmc-13457728: Can bio-hydrogen compete with bio-methane? Anaerobic digestion's unequal energy pathways weighed. Anna Sikora and Anna Detman-Ignatowska compare them. The 2026 Europe PMC paper is bioenergy. It weighs bio-H2 against bio-CH4 chances across the energy pathways with care.
pmc-13458828: A safe entry zone for ventral thoracic pathologies — the Konakondla-Telfeian-Shen pyramid. Sanjay Konakondla, Shailen G Sampath, Isaac Lee, and others define the corridor. The 2026 Europe PMC paper is neurosurgery. It maps a pyramid-shaped path to the thoracic spine.
pmc-13458928:
Juri Iwata, Masanori Yamamoto, and a large OCEAN-TAVI investigator group examined in 2026 how patients on hemodialysis fare after transcatheter aortic valve replacement with current devices. Dialysis patients are known to do poorly after this valve procedure, yet results with the newest devices have been unclear. The registry supplied 760 dialysis patients and 3,928 patients not on dialysis.

Before matching, one-year death rates were far higher in the dialysis group. Once 490 pairs were matched on baseline traits, mortality was nearly identical between groups, and stroke and heart failure readmission also matched. Dialysis itself still predicted death in the unmatched analysis, pointing to the heavy burden of other illnesses these patients carry.
pmc-13460228:
Fanghao Liu and colleagues tested in 2026 a simple trick to prevent collapsed lung during needle localization of lung nodules before surgery. Injecting numbing fluid just outside the chest lining and inserting the needle on the gravity-dependent side, where lung tissue rests against the chest wall, formed the combined strategy. Their Kunming study covered 166 patients localized and operated on between June and November 2024, split into four groups by which elements they received.

Collapsed lung struck half the patients receiving neither element, yet only one of thirty-three patients receiving both. Each element independently cut the odds sharply in adjusted models. Patients given the fluid also reported far less pain, with over half feeling none at all. The authors recommend the paired technique for routine localization work.
pmc-13461428:
Ebru Güzel Kuyucu and Nurettin Göksu Çini surveyed in 2026 four hundred four football fans in three Turkish cities. They asked about collective narcissism among supporters, the inflated belief that one's own fan group is superior, and its link to dysfunctional behavior. Face-to-face surveys during the 2025-2026 season also measured how fans rated the stadium atmosphere. They captured schadenfreude, the pleasure taken in a rival's misfortune, with local versus distant fans accounted for.

Collective narcissism predicted worse behavior directly. A richer perceived stadium atmosphere weakened that link, acting as a brake, while that pleasure strengthened it, acting as an accelerant. Distant fans behaved better than locals overall. The model explained a little over a third of the spread, and the authors suggest clubs work on atmosphere quality and rivalry culture rather than only policing individuals.
pmc-13461728:
Lim and colleagues measured a 2026 study of quality of life in Russian children with inflammatory bowel disease at a Moscow university clinic. The disease, Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis, burdens daily life beyond gut symptoms alone. Biologic drugs have improved control, but their link to children's lived experience was poorly defined.

One hundred and five children aged eight to seventeen took part, fifty-nine with Crohn's disease and forty-six with ulcerative colitis. Lim used three questionnaires covering disease specific quality of life, general quality of life, and family functioning. No significant differences appeared between biologic treated and conventionally treated children on any total score. Scores also matched between the two disease types, though emotional functioning scored lowest and social functioning highest across groups.
pmc-13461928:
Camilla Heldbjerg Drabe and co-authors describe a Danish family in which a brand new variant of the immune gene STAT3 causes hyper-IgE syndrome. The disorder brings recurrent staph abscesses and eczema, with strikingly different severity across five generations. The variant swaps one amino acid at position 417 and appears in no population database. In their 2026 study, lab tests on patient cells resolved conflicting computer predictions. The altered protein still bound DNA normally, but its response to the IL-6 signal was reduced, a partial rather than total loss of function.

Patient immune cells also failed to suppress an inflammatory molecule properly under IL-10, matching the partial defect. Clinically, relatives carrying the variant shared the syndrome's skin infections, eczema, and facial features, yet extra features like retained baby teeth varied markedly between them. Subtle partial defects, invisible to simple dominance tests, can still cause the full syndrome, the authors show.
pmc-13462428:
Tian Lin and colleagues build and test, in a 2026 lab study, a two-target antibody for neuroblastoma, the most common solid tumor outside the skull in children. Standard antibody treatment aims at a surface marker, GD2, yet some tumors escape by losing that marker or resisting treatment. Their antibody, G/R-001, grabs GD2 and a second marker, ROR1. Cells carrying either marker could be attacked, widening the net.

The antibody was produced in human cells and checked for structure. Binding tests showed strong attachment to both targets on real cancer cells. In killing tests it destroyed target cells more effectively than either single-target antibody. Cells carrying both markers died most, with killing above eighty percent at the top dose. The authors suggest the dual design may also rally natural killer immune cells. All results come from lab dishes, a first step before animal and patient studies.
pmc-13462728:
Abir Aldhalimi and co-authors argue, in a 2026 viewpoint article, that United States rules for artificial intelligence in mental health care are splintering by state and need a federal floor. Mental health needs keep rising, among young people, while provider shortages leave many without care. Chatbots and AI tools rushed into that gap after 2022. With no federal framework, states have begun writing their own laws. The team read the texts of four states: Illinois, Utah, New York, and Nevada.

 One regulates how AI is used in clinical settings, while the other regulates the technology itself, and some states blend both. Each leaves holes: protections vary by state, and developers, clinicians, and sellers face uncertain duties. Since mental health AI spans clinic and consumer use, neither approach alone covers the risks. The authors call for a federal baseline, sorted by risk, that keeps protections even nationwide.
pmc-13462928:
Anne-Sophie M C Marques leads a 2026 chemical biology study building tools to destroy a protein called NUDT5 inside cells. The tools help reveal how it shapes response to the leukemia drug 6-thioguanine. The drug needs activation inside the cell, and a sister protein trimming its active forms was known. Genome-wide knockout screens flagged NUDT5 as a key mediator of the drug's toxicity. The team built degrader molecules that drag NUDT5 to the cell's disposal system.

The degraders were checked for binding, three-part complex formation, speed of protein loss, and effects across the protein set. Removing the NUDT5 protein changed drug response in a way blocking its enzyme action would not predict, pointing to a scaffolding role beyond chemistry. The authors say the split between enzyme action and protein presence matters for combining this drug class in patients.
pmc-13463628:
Oisakede and colleagues mapped in 2026 what helps and what blocks near-infrared photoimmunotherapy. The treatment pairs an antibody carrying a light-sensitive dye with laser-like light. It kills tumor cells precisely where the light falls. Their scoping review followed standard mapping guidelines across five databases. It focused on the only version in clinical use, an epidermal growth factor receptor targeted drug approved first in Japan.

The 28 eligible studies showed the treatment kills cancer cells only where light reaches. Success concentrated in recurrent head and neck cancers. Doctors can reach those tumors with endoscopes and imaging guidance. Repeat sessions caused no accumulating harm. The main barriers were physical, since light penetrates tissue poorly. Deep or widespread tumors therefore stay out of reach. The method also needs specialized equipment and trained teams. Most side effects stayed local and manageable, though rare serious complications appeared in case reports.
pmc-13463928:
Lomangino and colleagues tested in 2026 whether image features from PET/CT scans can predict hidden lymph node spread in early-stage lung cancer. Patients staged as node-negative sometimes prove to have cancer in nodes after surgery, a surprise called nodal upstaging that changes treatment. All patients were scanned and treated at one institution with identical protocols.

The team extracted first- and second-level texture features from the scans and trained a machine learning model to flag patients with occult node disease. Using one center kept scan settings uniform, removing a common source of noise in such studies. The authors argue that a homogeneous, if small, dataset is the right way to find a reliable signal. Once refined, such a model could personalize the diagnostic path and the surgical plan for each patient.
pmc-13464328:
Alper Özkök and four colleagues published this 2026 postmortem case-control study of men who died of ischemic heart disease. They asked what the hearts look like when sildenafil, the erectile dysfunction drug, is found in the body. Erectile dysfunction and cardiovascular disease share roots, but the cardiac profile of users was unknown. Among 154 men, 77 sildenafil-positive cases faced age-matched controls on autopsy and toxicology findings.

Acute findings did not differ: neither coronary clots nor heart-muscle ischemia were more common in the positive group. Chronic damage was heavier: coronary disease, heart failure, bypass surgery, heavier hearts and coronary calcification all ran higher among sildenafil-positive men. After adjusting for other cardiovascular factors, only coronary calcification stayed linked, with about 2.6-fold odds. The authors read calcification as a marker of the vascular disease behind erectile dysfunction and heart disease, and counsel cardiovascular risk checks for users.
pmc-13465128:
Mu and colleagues tested in 2026 whether tannin from Caragana korshinskii, a shrub used as forage in northern China, protects sheep stomach lining cells from bacterial toxin injury. The rumen lining absorbs nutrients and shields the body, but a toxin called lipopolysaccharide can inflame and damage it in intensively fed animals.

Cells pretreated with the tannin before toxin exposure showed less injury across several measures. Inflammatory responses were weaker, oxidative damage was lower, and fewer cells died by apoptosis, a controlled cell death process. The protection tracked with reduced activity of a signaling chain that starts at the TLR4 receptor and drives inflammation. The authors conclude the tannin eased toxin injury under their lab conditions, a result that could inform feed additive research for sheep.
pmc-13466228:
Nava and colleagues reviewed in 2026 which implant choice works better after skin-reducing mastectomy, a surgery for women with large or sagging breasts that allows single-stage implant reconstruction. Placing the implant in front of the chest muscle avoids muscle dissection but needs healthy skin flaps. Placing it behind the muscle gives reliable coverage at the cost of pain and animation deformity, where the breast moves with the muscle.

Under PRISMA guidelines, they pooled twenty-six studies with 863 patients and 1,106 reconstructions, 432 prepectoral and 674 retropectoral. The pooled complication rate was similar, at twenty percent for prepectoral and twenty-five percent for retropectoral placement, and no single complication, from implant loss to skin necrosis, differed significantly. Patient-reported BREAST-Q scores favored prepectoral placement across satisfaction and wellbeing domains, though not by a clear margin. The authors suggest prepectoral placement may be preferred when flaps allow.
pmc-13466528:
Kuroda and co-authors asked in 2026 whether Japanese towns keeping senior prevention programs running through COVID-19 saw slower growth in care needs. Japan's long-term care insurance certifies need through a standard national process, and towns run local programs in five areas, from exercise to nutrition. The study linked a 2021 town survey to certification rates from 2018 to 2023. Of 1,741 towns invited, 1,114 entered the main analysis.

Full delivery was rare. Only about 16 percent of towns fully ran their exercise programs as planned for 2020, and about 14 percent did so for brain training. Towns fully delivering exercise programs saw certification rates rise more slowly during the pandemic years. The gap was about a tenth of a percentage point against towns that fell short. Brain training showed a similar protective gap. Other areas showed no clear pattern. The authors read this as evidence that keeping community prevention alive in a crisis pays off.
pmc-13466628:
Alessandro Conforti and colleagues follow knee arthritis patients starting the weight-loss drug semaglutide, tracking far more than body weight, in a 2026 real-world study. Ninety-three adults in routine rheumatology care began the drug, and eighty-eight finished six months of follow-up. Pain, daily function scores, body measures, inflammation markers, blood sugar, and fats were all recorded.

Each patient served as their own comparison, with no untreated group alongside. The authors therefore call every link they find non-causal, a caution stated up front. Modeling weighed weight lost against the highest dose reached, and a clustering step grouped patients into response patterns that paired joint relief with metabolic change in different mixes.
pmc-13466728:
Jia-Feng Duan, Tian Li, Qiu-Juan Zhang, and Jia-Hui Lu report a woman treated at once for an aggressive breast cancer and a hormone-secreting pituitary tumor, in a 2026 case report. The fifty-six-year-old had lived with a prolactinoma for five years, its hormone output held normal by medicine, when a painless breast lump present for two years proved to be invasive HER2-positive cancer.

Imaging had flagged only a tiny spiked nodule, and biopsy confirmed cancer that had already reached an armpit node. Given the node's involvement, the tumor's closeness to the nipple, and her refusal of breast-conserving surgery, she chose full mastectomy. No guideline covers pairing dual HER2 therapy with ongoing pituitary treatment, a gap the authors highlight.
pmc-13466928:
Bin Zhang, Zhen Yang, and Xiquan Zhang report pulling two long-abandoned vein filters out through blood vessels even though parts of them pierced into the duodenum, in a 2026 case report. Filters in the inferior vena cava stop clots traveling to the lungs, but devices left past their removal window cause rising harm. These two had sat for nine and eight years.

Both patients came with upper belly pain, and a scope showed filter parts poking into the bowel. Open surgery has been the usual answer given bleeding and bowel injury risks. The team's new vessel-based technique succeeded in both extreme cases, and they detail the steps and cautions for others facing the same trap.
pmc-13467128:
Pavelescu, Curici, and Călin critically review methods for detecting two reactive oxygen molecules in living mammalian systems in this 2026 paper. Hydrogen peroxide and superoxide act as useful signals at low levels but damage tissue when they build up. A widely used dye, DCFH-DA, has long been the default probe, yet it reacts with many substances and can mislead.

Covering work from 2015 to 2026, the authors compare five measurement platforms, from spin-trapping spectroscopy and fluorescent probes to genetically encoded sensors inside cells. Boronate-based probes have largely replaced the old dye for hydrogen peroxide imaging, the review finds. No single method wins on every measure. Selectivity, sensitivity, and resolution all matter. So the authors insist claims should rest on at least two complementary approaches, rather than one probe alone.
pmc-13467428:
Ruiying Wang and co-authors review in 2026 how China handles aluminum dross, the hazardous residue left when aluminum is melted and refined. Dross holds harmful substances such as aluminum nitride, fluorides, and chlorides, yet it also contains recoverable metal and alumina. The review pulls together the sources, makeup, and risks of the waste, then compares treatment options.

Cleanup methods aim to strip out nitrogen, fluorine, and chlorine compounds, using either water-based or heat-based routes. First-round dross can give back metallic aluminum, while the leaner second-round residue can feed refractory bricks, building materials, water-treatment agents, or alumina recovery. The authors weigh the strengths and limits of each route, framing dross as both an environmental liability and a resource stream worth mining.
pmc-13467628:
Haonan Qiu and co-authors develop in 2026 a lipid nanoparticle that carries imperatorin, a plant coumarin with antioxidant and anti-aging promise that dissolves poorly in water and is badly absorbed when swallowed. The carriers were built from grape seed oil and a food-grade fat, then squeezed through a high-pressure homogenizer. The finished particles were uniform spheres about 187 nanometers wide.

The carriers held nearly all of their cargo, with encapsulation efficiency of 99.54 percent in the reported tests. They stayed stable in simulated stomach fluid and released about 90.56 percent of the drug over 48 hours in simulated intestinal fluid. The team also built a two-cell gut model with a mucus layer to watch the particles cross, and checked safety and blood levels in animals. Their results indicate the carrier markedly improves how much imperatorin gets through.
pmc-13467928:
Shi and colleagues test how the dose of a single cycling session affects thinking skills in children with autism spectrum disorder, in 2026 exercise science research. Executive function covers mental control skills such as stopping impulses and holding information in mind. Thirty children completed a sedentary control session plus four cycling sessions: low or moderate intensity, lasting 20 or 40 minutes, with intensity tracked by heart rate. Computer tasks then measured impulse control and working memory.

Exercise condition changed reaction times and accuracy on the go/no-go impulse task, with the joint inhibitory-control score showing the strongest effect. Moderate-intensity sessions produced the clearest benefits, beating the sedentary condition in head-to-head comparisons. Working memory results were less consistent across the doses tested. Shi argues that brief moderate cycling could serve as a handy pre-activity primer for autistic children, while noting the dose details need work.
pmc-13468328:
Nurlan Almas and co-authors review in 2026 cadmium sulfide materials that kill bacteria with light, an approach gaining urgency as antibiotic resistance spreads through water and food chains. Cadmium sulfide absorbs visible light and generates reactive oxygen species that attack microbes; it can also release cadmium ions and physically disrupt membranes. The review maps how crystal form, particle shape from quantum dots to branched structures, and synthesis route set those behaviors.

A detailed tabulated analysis spans three material classes: plain cadmium sulfide, two-component composites, and three-part Z-scheme heterostructures that separate charges more cleverly. Computer calculations and molecular docking add mechanistic support. The authors also face the obvious challenges, including the toxicity of cadmium itself, and chart what must be solved before light-activated antibacterial coatings can be trusted in real water and food settings.
pmc-13468428:
Yaru Sun and co-authors test in 2026 a blast-resistant sandwich panel built around a self-adhesive stiffened polyimide foam between steel faces. Sandwich panels protect vehicles and structures from explosions, but their commonest failure is the face sheets peeling off the core. The self-adhesive foam was designed to grip the steel and resist that debonding. Blast experiments were paired with computer simulations of the dynamic response.

The foam itself proved thermally tough, keeping more than 36.2 percent of its mass at 800 degrees Celsius. Under blasts at the closer test distance, the new panel center displaced only 8.5 millimeters against 15.0 millimeters for a panel with plain polyimide foam, a 43.3 percent improvement. At the farther distance, displacement was 6.7 millimeters. The authors present the adhesive stiffened core as a practical upgrade for protective structures that cannot afford face-core separation.
pmc-13468928:
Andrea Hållstam, Charlotte Angelhoff, and Linda Gellerstedt report a qualitative study, published in 2026. It explores how people with chronic pain experience pain and sleep together. The authors interviewed patients in groups and individually. All had completed a pain rehabilitation programme in Sweden. It was an interdisciplinary programme. The accounts were analysed thematically.

Patients described a vicious circle. Pain and poor sleep fed each other. The two were hard to pull apart. Consequences were practical, emotional, and social. Daily life suffered in all three ways. Rehabilitation should pay more direct attention to sleep, the authors conclude. Sleep hygiene deserves focus. So does sleep ergonomics, the physical set-up for sleeping. This sits within a holistic approach to chronic pain.
pmc-13469228:
Roisin O’Donovan and a large Irish team umbrella-review in 2026 the research on human milk banking services, the systems that collect donated breast milk for infants whose mothers cannot supply it. An umbrella review synthesizes existing systematic reviews rather than single studies. Following recognized evidence synthesis guidance, the team searched seven databases plus grey literature for work published between 2000 and June 2025, screening with two independent reviewers.

Thirteen reviews were identified, covering milk banks in middle- and high-income countries and the donors, recipient families, and staff who keep them running. The authors note how little standardized information exists on governance, quality, and sustainability criteria, the very things a bank needs to supply milk consistently and equitably. Their synthesis will feed a co-designed evidence framework for setting up and scaling milk bank services, a resource new banks currently reinvent country by country.
pmc-13469428:
Hu and colleagues measured brain activity in this 2026 study to test whether natural sounds improve the emotional state of psychiatric healthcare workers, a group under heavy daily stress. Forty participants listened to birdsong, insect sounds, and rain sounds while electroencephalography, a scalp recording of brain waves, tracked emotional indicators before and after each exposure.

Birdsong lowered stress readings and raised relaxation scores among the workers. Insect sounds reduced directed attention, while rain sounds reduced engagement with the task at hand. At the same time, insect and rain sounds produced significantly higher scores on the study's engagement and interest indices than birdsong did. The authors conclude that short exposure to natural sounds can shift measured emotional states in a positive direction for this stressed workforce.
pmc-13469728:
Korkmaz examines how the chemotherapy drug methotrexate stresses ovarian cancer cells in this 2026 laboratory study. The drug mainly blocks the folate pathway, but it also creates oxidative stress, damage from reactive oxygen molecules, which pushes cells toward self-destruction. Working with OVCAR-3 cells, a standard ovarian cancer cell line, the author tested whether four antioxidant compounds could soften these effects.

After 24 hours, methotrexate lowered the cells' antioxidant capacity while raising oxidant levels and a marker of fat damage. Two protective proteins, Nrf2 and HO-1, also fell. Meanwhile, signals for the cell's built-in death program rose. Those included a higher Bax to Bcl-2 ratio and active caspase enzymes. Adding antioxidants partly restored balance and calmed the death signals, with resveratrol showing the strongest effect among the doses tested.
pmc-13469828:
Charlotte Spurway and colleagues report in 2026 a qualitative study of how brace and wheelchair users in Cambodia reach rehabilitation services. Access to such care is a recognized human right, yet shortages of staff and fragmented services limit it in many poorer countries. Seventeen current or former patients of a Phnom Penh rehabilitation center, aged eighteen to sixty five, described their experiences in translated interviews.

Three themes organize the accounts: early illness and care seeking, the routes taken to obtain a brace or wheelchair, and the effect of finally receiving one. Participants described long delays and uneven experiences with medical care and physiotherapy along the way. Even so, the devices proved central to daily life and independence. The authors use the accounts to show where service pathways break down.
pmc-13470328:
Matevž Rumpret and co-authors report in 2026 a strep protein that hides during lab growth yet becomes a target of protection during real infection. Vaccine hunters usually study surface proteins that bacteria show in culture flasks. The protein Slr sits in every strain of Streptococcus pyogenes, the cause of strep throat and invasive disease, but it does not appear on cells grown in broth.

Experiments showed a zinc sensing regulator keeps Slr switched off until zinc runs low, as happens inside a host. Antibodies against Slr protected mice in both passive transfer and vaccination tests against invasive infection. Human and mouse antibody responses to Slr matched those against the classic M protein. Oddly, the response focused on one repeated motif region, which the authors read as a possible escape trick.
pmc-13470728:
Yu Qiao and eight colleagues published this 2026 study of gas held in deep coal on the eastern edge of China's Ordos Basin. Deep coalbed methane is a cleaner fuel trapped in coal seams more than 2,000 metres down. The team studied how the gas sits in the coal, and how its carbon isotopes, slightly different forms of carbon, shift as gas escapes. They used both field desorption tests and computer models of coal molecules.

In the field tests, the ratio of free gas to adsorbed gas, gas stuck to coal surfaces, ranged from 0.94 to 2.22 during release. The methane isotope values were generally heavy and grew heavier across temperature stages. The simulations showed free gas sitting in large pores and cracks, while small pores held both free and adsorbed gas. They also showed the isotope forms moving at different speeds, which explains the shift seen in the field.
pmc-13471328:
Pipatkullachart and colleagues at a Thai medical center tested whether a home-grown hospital guideline could cut needless follow-up visits for newborns with jaundice, a yellowing of the skin caused by bilirubin buildup. Their 2026 before-and-after study compared care in the six months before the guideline with the six months after it. The study covered 274 babies born at 35 weeks or later who went home without light therapy.

Follow-up visits dropped sharply once the guideline took effect: 34.3% of babies in the later group needed a return visit, compared with 49.6% in the earlier group. Readmissions barely moved, affecting 3.6% of babies after the change versus 2.9% before it, a gap the authors judged not meaningful. The team concludes that adapting global guidance to local needs can trim wasted visits without early signs of harm.
pmc-13472928:
Chen and colleagues present a 2026 systematic review of artificial intelligence for spotting osteoporosis in scans taken for other reasons. Bone thinning often goes undetected until a fracture, and the standard bone density test is hard to access. Opportunistic screening lets AI read routine images for bone health at no extra scan cost. The team followed standard review methods across three databases to February 2026.

Fifty-seven studies were included, most of them retrospective and from single centers. CT scans were the most used image source, with models judged mainly by discrimination scores for osteoporosis, low bone mass, and fracture risk. The review also mapped why results vary so much between studies. The pattern is promising but immature: before hospitals trust AI bone checks on every scan, the field needs shared standards and prospective, multi-center proof.
pmc-13473028:
Sutaşır and co-authors review what emergency physicians need to know when nuclear medicine scans and treatments go wrong, from tracer leaking out of the vein to allergic reactions. Their 2026 narrative review searched four databases for studies from 2020 to 2024 on acute events after radiopharmaceutical administration.
