Yaqing Lin leads a 2026 report of a new HIV variant found in Guangdong, southern China. When several HIV strains circulate together, they can swap gene segments and create recombinant forms. Surveillance for drug resistance before treatment picked up unusual strains among men who have sex with men.

Near-complete genomes from four people defined a new circulating form, CRF209_cpx, built from three parents: CRF01_AE, CRF07_BC, and subtype B. Family-tree analysis dated its origin to between 2011 and 2013. A fifth strain mixed the new form with subtype B again. No passed-on drug resistance appeared in the five sequences. Most used the CXCR4 entry route into cells. The authors call for stronger molecular surveillance in this population.
pmc-13576328:
Yaxian Shi, Guiling Huang, and Jeannette M Beasley survey where health workers in China get nutrition information, in a 2026 study. They also ask how those sources link to how competent staff feel giving nutrition advice. Patients trust clinicians on food questions, yet many staff had little nutrition training. The survey covered 450 professionals, two-thirds of them nurses.

Colleagues were the most used source, followed by social media, then professional websites. Median self-rated competence sat at 120 on the scale used. Checking colleagues more often, asking friends or family, and joining webinars or continuing courses each linked to higher self-ratings. The link for informal sources caught the authors' attention, since confidence drawn from weak sources may mislead. They frame the work as a prompt to improve access to solid nutrition guidance.
pmc-13578328:
Abdirisak Mohamed Yousuf, Deepa Krishnan, and Zubeda Ukundimana link shifting rain to failing water quality in the Mubuku River basin of western Uganda, in a 2026 study. The team tracked ten years of rain records, from 2014 to 2024, and paired a standard drought index with mapped lab tests of river water.

Both dry years and heavy runoff years left the water worse, through two routes. Dry spells let minerals build up in slow flow, while wet spells washed farm and town waste into the river. Dissolved solids climbed by about a third, hardness rose, and germ counts passed safe limits at several sites. Three sampling spots ran far dirtier than the basin average. The authors urge action aimed at those hotspots, timed to the seasons.
pmc-13578428:
Amit Kumar and Sujata Jadhav model how reliably a sensor run hydroponic farm keeps working, in a 2026 study. Soil free farms stack sensors, controllers, and pumps, and a failure in any part can kill a crop. Steady uptime matters most where water and land are scarce. Their math model walks the system through working, worn, and failed states over time.

Two nature inspired search methods then tuned the setup for uptime. A swarm method and a gene based method each pushed availability near ninety eight percent in their runs, with small gaps set by tuning choices. The authors offer the pair of tools as a planning aid, helping growers set repair schedules and pick settings before breakdowns bite.
pmc-13578828:
Gabriel Reis Alves Carneiro and colleagues build a lab test for retatrutide, a new long acting hormone drug, aimed at anti-doping work. The drug acts on three gut hormone switches at once and reshapes body weight and metabolism, which draws off label use among active people. Four users who dosed themselves under the skin twice gave blood and urine samples over set times for the study.

The method, built on precise mass reading of liquid samples, passed sport authority checks for reliability. In urine the intact drug never showed up, despite several extraction tries. Blood levels rose and fell in waves, hinting at slow release from the injection depot. Traces stayed findable in blood for about eight weeks after the first dose, so the authors urge blood based testing for this drug class.
pmc-13579828:
Sebastian Sanchez-Lopez and colleagues draw lessons from a Lassa fever case that surfaced in the Midwest of the United States, in a 2026 review. Lassa is a rodent borne viral fever rooted in West Africa, where models now project millions of infections a year, most mild yet some deadly. A traveler case far from that region exposed how slowly rich health systems can spot a rare, high stakes fever.

Early signs mimic common ills, and skipping the travel history delays the call. Lab confirmation leans on gene tests whose reach bends with viral variety and timing. The standard drug rests on thin, mixed proof, while vaccines and antibody drugs remain out of reach for routine care. The authors map gaps in spotting, testing, and treating such imports, and urge rehearsed readiness before the next one lands.
pmc-13580428:
Badawy and co-authors systematically review the skin injuries caused by radiation during brain and spine catheter procedures, in this 2026 paper. Long fluoroscopy runs can concentrate high doses on one patch of skin. Following PRISMA 2020 methods across four databases, they gathered case reports, case series, and other studies that reported a skin reaction, a relevant dose, or both.

Twenty-five studies covering roughly 686 patients in eleven countries qualified. Hair loss dominated the reports, appearing in 21 studies, while dermatitis and redness appeared in four and ulceration or tissue death in two. Cohort incidence ranged from about 5 to 56 percent, climbing with dose and complexity. Temporary hair loss clustered near the known threshold of roughly 3 gray, appearing two to five weeks post-procedure, whereas ulcers surfaced months to years later. The authors demand standard peak skin dose reporting.
pmc-13584428:
Arghavan Zebardast and Kasra Javadi review what Epstein-Barr virus does to the body's microbial communities in this 2026 paper. The virus infects most people for life and links to several cancers and immune diseases. Whether it also reshapes the bacteria living in the mouth, gut, and other niches was far less clear, so the pair searched three large databases for human studies.

Nine studies from 2017 to 2025 fit, covering the mouth, nose passage, gut, stomach tissue, and gum pockets. Where the virus or its linked diseases were present, microbial mixes differed in ways that changed from niche to niche. Measures of community variety, though, pointed in mixed directions across studies. The authors warn that all the work was watch-only and small, so no cause can be claimed yet.
pmc-13585428:
Davinia Beaver, Adrian C. Cioanca, and Nigel L. Barnett grow light-sensing eye cells in a flat dish in this 2026 study. Eye diseases such as retinitis pigmentosa kill photoreceptors, the cells that turn light into signals. Labs usually grow replacements in 3D clumps called organoids, which are slow and hard to scale. The team instead used a flat 2D method with a human stem cell line fitted with glowing markers for eye development.

Fed with set chemicals, the cells turned on the right marker genes in order and built early inner and outer segment shapes. By day 42, most cells carried key photoreceptor proteins, and gene reads showed the flat route matured faster than organoids. The authors pitch it as a quicker, animal-free path toward cell therapy and drug screening, pending more checks.
pmc-13590328:
Teo Susnjak and four colleagues map a long dispute about lasting symptoms after Lyme disease, the tick borne infection. One camp reads lasting fatigue and pain as a post treatment syndrome, while the other sees signs of an infection that never fully cleared. The team sorted a large set of papers from 2000 to 2024 with help from language models. They then checked key trials and lab studies in full.

Patterns split by study type: reports and lab work leaned one way, while trials and guidance leaned the other. Trial audits showed some short term gains that faded or varied by outcome. Lab findings hinted at ways germs might persist, yet did not prove live infection causes human symptoms. Susnjak and the team urge care in stretching lab claims into clinic claims.
pmc-13591728:
Jason A Miller and four colleagues recount, in 2026, a young American man whose chest pain was first blamed on repeat inflammation around the heart. Acute rheumatic fever, an immune reaction after untreated strep throat, has grown rare in the United States, which lets it hide. At a Boston hospital his heart enzyme levels ran high, and a heart MRI showed muscle inflammation. No valve damage appeared on scans.

Wandering joint aches then prompted blood tests for strep antibodies, and both markers came back high. With heart inflammation as a major sign and joint aches plus raised inflammation as minor ones, he met the standard Jones criteria. Miller and the team urge keeping rheumatic fever in mind and using heart MRI when standard scans stay murky.
pmc-13592328:
Christian Zoister leads a 2026 team dressing supramolecular fibers with antiviral soap like molecules to block herpes simplex virus. Six new surfactants carry a sulfonate head tuned to grip viral coat proteins. Mixed with water loving fiber forming units, they coat the fibers at low share. Push the share too high and the fibers break into plain micelles, the team found by spectroscopy and microscopy.

Fibrous assemblies stopped the virus at far lower doses than the micellar forms. They also harmed human cells less, likely because the active heads sit locked in the scaffold. Exchange tests showed looser, more dynamic assemblies worked better. Zoister and colleagues present co assembly as a way to aim many weak grips at a virus at once.
pmc-13592628:
Sarah Covasso leads a team listening to French adolescents and their parents living with suspected Lyme disease. The tick borne infection can be hard to pin down, and families endure long stretches of medical doubt. Across several centers, paired interviews with teens and parents ran from March to June 2023, and grounded theory sorted 809 coded passages into three themes.

Family history colored how each household read the illness. Parents and teens often split in their trust of medical advice, and teens voiced confusion, boredom with the topic, and fear that a dormant infection might return to harm them. A shared plea ran through the talks: clearer knowledge to crowd out misinformation. Covasso and the team urge stronger family doctor coordination with specialist centers.
pmc-13592828:
Viivi Virkkunen and three colleagues track women's sexual function across the retirement transition in Finland. Retirement reshapes daily life, stress, and health habits, all tied to sexual wellbeing, yet direct study was scarce. Their follow up covered 110 women averaging sixty three years old, drawn from a national retirement and aging cohort. A standard questionnaire scored total function and six parts, from desire to satisfaction, once a year before and after each woman retired.

Total scores held steady across the transition. Desire rose slightly but clearly, while lubrication dipped without reaching firm statistical ground. Arousal, orgasm, pain, and satisfaction all stayed flat. Virkkunen and the team read retirement as neutral overall for sexual function, with a small bright spot in desire worth longer study.
pmc-13592928:
Verma and colleagues report a 2026 study building the first survey tool that measures whether patients with advanced liver disease feel their care matches their goals. Patients and caregivers answered as pairs within a palliative care trial. The tool has two parts: a seven-item scale on whether clinicians discussed prognosis and goals, and a four-item scale on whether care fit the patient's preferences.

Statistical checks supported the tool's structure, and its scores behaved as expected against related measures. Higher scores on the conversation scale went with lower caregiver burden, a link that supports the idea that good goal talks ease family strain.  A tested measure lets clinics track whether care follows patient goals.
pmc-13593528:
Xinyi Wang and co-authors describe a patient whose fainting spells returned years after a first cardioneuroablation. The procedure burns small nerve clusters in the heart to calm the reflex behind vasovagal syncope. Their 2026 case report follows the man through a second, more complete ablation and explains why the first one failed.

Heart rhythm data showed that vagal nerve function had partly grown back five years after the first procedure, which had treated only the left atrium. During the repeat procedure the team used strong fractionated electrical signals to locate the active nerve clusters, and ablating the right inferior cluster proved central. Eighteen months later the patient had no further fainting or warning symptoms, and no complications occurred.
pmc-13612228:
Annette S Kim leads an eight-author team looking back on fifteen years of leukemia test standardization in 2026. Monitoring chronic myeloid leukemia means measuring BCR::ABL1 RNA precisely, and results from different laboratories must agree. The International Scale was created to harmonize reporting, but its real-world effect had never been fully assessed. The team mined a national proficiency testing program: over 200 laboratories, six samples a year, more than 5,500 results from 2009 to 2023.

Adoption climbed fast, from 8 percent of laboratories in 2009 to 86 percent by 2015 and over 99 percent by 2019. As it spread, the spread between laboratories shrank steadily, reaching a low near 0.2 standard deviations. The improvement correlated strongly with scale adoption at high, intermediate, and low transcript levels. Nothing else tracked the gains: not the reference gene chosen, not the reagent kit, not the assay type, not the practice setting. The authors conclude standardized reporting itself drove the precision.
pmc-13616828:
Doaa Mohamed Farahat Aboul Azm and colleagues soak dental ceramic discs for 28 days in three everyday liquids. They want to see which material keeps its colour better. The rivals are multi-layered zirconia and lithium disilicate glass ceramic. Crowns meet mouthwash, coffee, and cola daily, and staining can spoil a costly restoration. Thirty discs, two millimetres thick, were split between the two ceramics, then divided again among chlorhexidine rinse, cola, and coffee at room temperature.

Colour was read with a spectrophotometer at the start and every week for four readings after immersion began, and the shifts were calculated for each pairing. Pairwise comparisons show which ceramic shrugs off which drink. Dentists choosing between a layered zirconia crown and a pressed glass ceramic can quote patients something firmer than habit about how the shine will age.
pmc-13617628:
Laura Morato and nine colleagues ask how curvature shapes the cellular architecture of epithelial shells, the closed hollow layers that form an early stage of mammalian embryos. On flat sheets, cell neighbor patterns follow conserved rules, yet little was known about curved shells. The team built three-dimensional Voronoi models, a geometric way of tiling space, that predict shell organization for different cell counts.

Laboratory MDCK cysts with precise cell-by-cell segmentation matched the model predictions, and so did early mouse embryos. Higher curvature per cell patch demanded more pentagon-shaped cells to close the shell, echoing the geometry of natural cages. Small cysts and embryos used only a restricted subset of polygon arrangements, mainly those maximizing area relative to perimeter. The authors conclude that shell organization, while diverse, is fundamentally non-random, guided by geometry, curvature, and topology together.
pmc-13618928:
Minglin Xu and nine colleagues dissect ginseng dripping pills, a traditional Chinese patent medicine used widely for cardiovascular disease, to find its active ingredients and how they might work. Advanced mass spectrometry profiling identified one hundred thirteen compounds in the pills, of which thirteen were confirmed to enter the bloodstream, with ginsenosides, the signature ginseng chemicals, predominating. Network pharmacology then mapped those components onto disease targets for heart attack and atherosclerosis.

Eighteen core targets emerged, threaded through pathways including PI3K-Akt, RAS, cAMP, Rap1, and calcium signaling. Docking simulations placed the blood-absorbed ginsenosides snugly against three core targets, MAPK3, MMP9, and PTGS2. The authors conclude the pills likely protect the heart through a multicomponent, multitarget, multipathway mode of action typical of traditional formulas. They offer the integrated chemistry-plus-network approach as a template for giving such medicines a modern scientific footing.
pmc-13619628:
Marius G Braun and a large team of colleagues built a gel that forms only where tumor cells are metabolically active. Many tumors release lactate as a waste and signal molecule. Their material starts as a modified alginate that stays liquid until an enzyme turns that lactate into hydrogen peroxide. A second enzyme then uses the peroxide to link the chains into a soft solid.

Gels formed within minutes around tumor cell clusters, including one grown from a patient's brain tumor, and spread about a millimeter from the surface. Stiffness and polymer density faded with distance, creating a natural gradient. Protein profiling showed weaker growth signals and stronger signs tied to cell movement and matrix reshaping. The authors present metabolite-triggered gelation as a way to model how tumors and their surroundings push on each other.
pmc-13621628:
Ashley Hui Ying Teh, Shao Yuan Chong, and Eleanor J Ong argue that implementation science keeps communities as consultants when it should be building them into scientists. The field now embraces co-creation, yet the skills and infrastructure for research stay inside universities, leaving neighborhoods dependent on academic go-betweens to certify knowledge about their own lives. Training programs meant to spread capacity systematically pass communities by.

Drawing on a Singapore community research group, the authors show residents gaining real methodological skills when training is fused with advocacy and program work. Their proposal is the community-formed research ecosystem: standing local infrastructure that lets communities spot problems, adapt frameworks, gather and analyze data, and campaign on findings without waiting for outside investigators. Academics would shift into support roles. The payoff, they argue, is research capacity that survives after grants end, plus fairer distribution of who gets to produce knowledge.
pmc-13623128:
Mengyun Fu, Jiajin Wu, and Abbasali Sadeghi examine how Chinese university teachers actually spend their working time under the Double First-Class initiative, a national push to build world-class universities. The authors frame the problem as requisitioned time: hours claimed by duties that outrank the research teachers value most. Questionnaire data came from faculty across twelve provinces and municipalities.

Three patterns stand out. Undergraduate teaching forms a fixed, high-priority block that no one can move. Most teachers wish writing came first, yet paperwork and administration beat research in daily practice, which the authors trace to administrative power outweighing academic authority. The gap between the priority teachers want for research and the priority it gets is wide. To close it, the authors propose reforms at three levels of governance, from national policy down to the department, aimed at giving the academic profession a steadier future.
pmc-13624028:
Abiodun Mayowa Akanmu, writing alone, reviews the microbes of the whole cattle gut, not just the famous rumen. The rumen, the fermentation vat where microbes turn fibre into energy, dominates research, while the gut's later chambers are barely charted. The review separates solid knowledge from early guesses across each region.

Studies agree that each gut region filters its own microbial community, yet most data are one-time snapshots of gut contents rather than the wall lining. Gene presence is often mistaken for real activity. Calfhood adds a moving picture, as milk gives way to solid feed and each region matures on its own clock. The foregut still supplies most microbe-made energy, while downstream stretches handle leftovers, barrier defence, and immune contact in amounts nobody has pinned down. Akanmu calls for long-term, whole-tract studies that measure microbes and their products directly before feed interventions can be trusted.
pmc-13624228:
Felix R M Koenig leads the team introducing MOBCART, an MRI scoring add-on that grades the bone side of knee cartilage repairs. The established MOCART score covers the repair tissue broadly but skims the bone underneath, even though bone quality shapes whether these grafts last. MOBCART scores three bone features, integration, normalization, and cysts, on a fifty-point scale.

To test whether the score can be trusted, four readers of mixed experience, from senior specialists to residents, graded thirty-two postoperative scans from twenty-three patients, and two readers repeated the task later. Agreement on the total score was moderate to good across the whole group and good between the two experts, while agreement on the single features ran higher. Repeat scoring by the same reader was also strong. The authors present MOBCART as a reproducible companion to the standard score for reporting bone healing after knee repair.
pmc-13625228:
Elizabeth A M Michels and colleagues shadow nurses through real shifts to find which moments of the working day spark stress. At a German university hospital, trained observers logged events across an eight-hour shift for up to eighty-five nurses, rating stress on the spot. Chest sensors recorded heart rate variability, a beat-based gauge of strain, and events were sorted into direct care burden, organizational burden, and positive moments.

The study logged 1,617 events in all. Direct care burden drew the highest observer stress ratings and lower variability readings than paperwork-type burden, while positive events drew the calmest ratings. Everyday care tasks, more than office friction, appear to drive acute strain, which gives managers a clearer target when they redesign rosters and support.
pmc-13628528:
Julie Borel and three colleagues show that germylium ions, strongly electron-hungry germanium compounds, can strip fluorine and hydrogen from fluorinated alkanes, published in 2026. Breaking carbon-fluorine bonds matters because fluorinated chemicals are useful yet persistent, and recycling them needs chemistry that can open those very strong bonds.

The team isolated several germylium salts and related fluorine-bridged pairs, then used them to convert fluorocyclohexane cleanly into cyclohexene while releasing hydrogen gas. Calculations and experiments pointed to a single concerted step in which a companion germane acts as a base, a pathway unlike the stepwise route seen with silicon cousins. The contrast sharpens understanding of how these heavy main-group catalysts might be tuned for defluorination work.
pmc-13636028:
Kajsa Lidström Holmqvist and four colleagues mapped the research on drug-free rehabilitation for women after traumatic brain injury. Women experience somewhat different symptoms and life consequences from brain injury than men, yet rehabilitation research rarely separates them. The team searched three databases for studies of women aged eighteen to sixty-five. They kept studies where women formed at least half the participants or where women's results were reported separately.

Forty-one studies with varied designs qualified. The interventions fell into three families: alternative and complementary approaches, training aimed at restoring lost functions, and skills training to sharpen thinking, which held the most studies. Most work happened in community or outpatient settings. The striking finding is an absence: not one intervention was designed for women or adapted to women's needs. The authors call on the field to build and test rehabilitation with an explicit gender perspective.
pmc-13636128:
Geraldo Aleixo Passos and five colleagues published this 2026 review of how the thymus teaches T cells not to attack the body. Deep inside the thymus, medullary epithelial cells display a vast menu of self proteins to developing T cells. Two master regulators, Aire and Fezf2, switch on thousands of tissue-specific genes in those cells. What remained murky is the step between gene activity and the actual protein fragments loaded for display.

The review gathers new tools that read those displayed fragments directly from cells. It stresses that several layers, from protein cutting to loading, can uncouple fragment display from gene activity levels. Single-cell gene maps and fragment catalogues therefore complement each other rather than substitute. Putting both together should explain why tolerance fails in selective ways in autoimmune disease. The authors also argue the combined view can guide therapies aimed at specific self targets.
pmc-13638728:
Jaime Uy De Baron and two colleagues present a 2026 methods study on placing microscope images of bone tissue inside three-dimensional scans. Matching flat histology slices to scan volumes helps surgeons judge how wide a margin to cut around a bone tumor.

The authors tested two new geometric methods against an established one across thirty-eight dog specimen dissections. All three methods located slices with mean errors well under a millimeter in practical terms, and the freeform method performed best. They argue the low-cost approach can support treatment planning for bone sarcoma, a rare cancer that mainly affects young people.
pmc-13638828:
Ali Al Hatem and four colleagues published a 2026 worm study on how the diabetes drug metformin guards against mouth bacteria. These germs live in the mouth and do no harm there, but they release a bleach-like chemical that can kill the tiny worm used in this work.

Worms given metformin first survived the chemical far better, and more drug meant more protection. The effect needed SKN-1, a stress switch in the worm. Two partners were also required: the p38 MAPK pathway and a helper protein called MDT-15. The authors say metformin may deserve a look as a drug against these germs.
pmc-13639028:
Yingying Ma and eleven colleagues present a 2026 study on predicting how efficiently cells turn RNA messages into protein. Direct measurement of that step is costly, so the team tested whether software estimates from standard RNA sequencing could stand in for it.

Across fifteen datasets, the inferred translation profiles matched true ribosome measurements better than RNA levels alone. The approach also uncovered hidden cancer antigens that expression-based filters had missed. Applied to glioma, a brain cancer, it split patients into sharper risk groups. The authors present translation inference as a cheap upgrade for precision cancer care.
pmc-13639228:
Katrijn Hooyberghs and nine colleagues published a 2026 pig breeding study on whether a sire's genetic scores predict evenness and survival in his litters. Large litters produce more small piglets, and farmers hope selection on boars can counter that trend.

Six Piétrain boars with high or low breeding values were mated to ninety-three sows, producing 1,421 liveborn piglets followed to slaughter. The sire scores predicted litter uniformity only weakly, though links appeared for pre-weaning survival and growth evenness. Weight variation at weaning predicted later variation well, suggesting evenness before and after weaning behaves as two separate traits.
pmc-13645528:
Leilei Liu and ten colleagues present a systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis linking the triglyceride-glucose index with major heart and brain events in people with cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic syndrome. The index, built from two routine blood values, stands in for insulin resistance.

Eight cohort studies covering over two million participants and about 179 thousand events were pooled. People in the highest index band faced roughly a fifth higher event risk than those in the lowest, and risk climbed in a curved pattern with each index step. Subgroup checks agreed. The authors say the index may aid risk prediction, while causality still needs proof.
pmc-13646028:
Stewart Forsyth asks, in a 2026 essay, whether Europe should have its own shared policy on infant feeding. Everyone agrees breastfeeding matters, he notes, yet advice should rest on the strongest science and fit each family's situation. He presses a distinction between a factor merely linked with a health outcome and one proven to cause it. That difference, he argues, decides how firmly a policy can demand compliance.

Forsyth questions the worldwide push to breastfeed for two years or beyond, tracing it to a 1990 declaration meeting in Florence attended by few wealthy countries. In places with clean water, good food, and strong health care, he suggests, such a blanket rule may outrun its evidence and invite non-compliance. He frames policy as a moving process that should track how sure the science is and how family needs change over time.
pmc-13647128:
Summer Dieterle and three colleagues build a gene model for the fruit fly Drosophila funebris version of a transporter gene called ABCB7. Gene models spell out where a gene sits and how its parts are arranged, and they anchor comparisons across species. The work belongs to a growing dataset on how detoxification gene families evolved in one branch of the fly family tree. Students in a course-based research program carried out the annotation using an adapted partnership protocol.

The model was placed on a published genome assembly for the species and characterized against the well-studied version from Drosophila melanogaster. Such paired models let researchers ask whether detox genes keep their shape or diverge as species adapt to new foods and toxins. The paper is a data report, not a hypothesis test. Its value lies in adding one checked brick to the comparative wall the wider project is building.
pmc-13648128:
Published in 2026, a cross-sectional study by Miyoung Kim and two colleagues asks whether the meaning workers find in their work links traumatic experiences with posttraumatic growth in South Korea. Growth here means positive psychological change after hardship, and the study includes events that fall outside formal diagnostic criteria as well as those that meet them.

Surveys from 328 workers aged twenty or older were analysed with mediation models. Meaning of work carried a significant indirect link between total traumatic events and growth, and the same held for events outside diagnostic criteria but not for events meeting them. The authors suggest meaning-centred support could complement workplace mental health care, while noting that longitudinal work is still needed.
pmc-13649428:
Magdalena Brodowicz-Król and five colleagues asked if the feel of a work placement shapes the broad care skills of nurses who study while they work. The group covered 293 nurses in a master's course, with an average age near 43 and long work histories. Two survey scales scored their whole-person care skills and the quality of their practice setting.

Scores for care skills ran high, with ethics and growth at the top. A sense of belonging in the team scored lowest. All parts of the two scales rose and fell together, and chances to learn on the job tied most strongly to care skill. Age, sex, and background did not shift the scores. The authors stress good learning chances on the ward.
pmc-13649728:
Shaimaa A. M. Abdelmohsen and colleagues compared oils drawn from black and white pepper, the dried fruit of a common spice vine. Pepper oils hold plant chemicals with known health effects in folk use. The team pulled the oils with a solvent system, read their make-up with a gas tool, and tested them on germs and on free radicals.

Black pepper gave a higher oil yield than white. Both oils fought free radicals strongly, at near the same high rate. Black pepper oil beat white against a common soil germ in dish tests. The black oil proved rich in the sharp compound piperine and a related alkaloid, while sterols led the white oil. Total alkaloids sat near a third of each oil.
pmc-13650428:
Yuzheng Zhang and three colleagues build a stricter test bench for computer models that predict colorectal cancer from gut microbe data. Most such models are graded on random splits that mix samples from the same study or country into both training and testing, which can leak shortcuts and inflate scores.

From a pool of source samples the team curated close to two thousand cancer or healthy samples spanning 15 studies and 10 countries, holding precancerous adenoma samples aside as an extra challenge. Four model types were graded under random splits, leave-one-study-out, and leave-one-country-out rules. Scores fell under the harder rules, microbe profiles could themselves predict which study a sample came from, and balancing tricks gave limited help. Probability cleanup steps improved reliability somewhat, while uncertainty-based refusal to answer beat random refusal. The bench is offered as a reality check for the field.
pmc-13651528:
Xue Wang and ten colleagues demonstrate an organic framework that charges in sunlight and pays the charge back in the dark, a single material doing the jobs of solar cell and battery. Most light-storing materials are metal-based, while purely organic versions are rare despite their design flexibility.

The material is a crystalline layered framework built around bipyridine units. Light drives a proton-assisted one-electron reduction of those units, and the stored electrons sit stably when oxygen is excluded. Its photoinduced voltage is the most negative yet reported for an organic material of this kind. On demand, the charge can leave as electricity for an aqueous solar battery, or reduce oxygen to hydrogen peroxide. With a platinum helper, it can also release hydrogen gas in darkness, a first for this framework family. Spectroscopic detective work maps the storage mechanism for future designs.
pmc-13652528:
Ricardo Limongi writes an editorial on how artificial intelligence is changing clinical judgment in nursing. Prediction scores, sepsis alerts, and electronic records that suggest next steps already operate at the bedside, and nurses receive and act on most of those signals. Yet nurses, he notes, have had the least say in how these tools are designed and judged, a gap he calls paradoxical.

Limongi argues the debate should move past accuracy scores toward the design of collaboration between nurse and machine. Good hybrid intelligence, in his account, means systems built so that professional judgment stays in charge. With alerts and suggestions fitted to real nursing work rather than added on top of it. The piece is a call to involve nurses early, before tools harden into daily infrastructure that shapes care without their input.
pmc-4702828:
Vizcaíno, Csordas, del-Toro, and their colleagues updated the PRIDE database in 2016. PRIDE is one of the world's leading stores for mass spectrometry proteomics data, the protein measurements from many labs. Since early 2014, the PRIDE Archive has been its new storage system.

The update describes the archive and the tools linked to it for submitting, browsing, and reusing data. Public proteomics data let other teams re-check findings and combine studies. Standard submission also forces clearer records of how each dataset was made. PRIDE's growth mirrors the field's shift toward open data as a norm in protein research.
pmc-5552828:
Rena, Hardie, and Pearson reviewed the mechanisms of action of metformin in 2017. Metformin is the world's most used diabetes drug, prized for how it improves glucose control and cuts diabetes-related harm. How it achieves those benefits is complex and, after decades of use, still not fully pinned down.

In the body, its best-known action is to cut hepatic glucose production, the liver's release of sugar into the blood. The authors weigh evidence on its molecular targets and its wider effects on the gut and metabolism. Metformin remains the first-line treatment for type two diabetes worldwide. Knowing how it works helps design safer successors and explains its possible benefits beyond blood sugar.
pmc-6041728:
Neil Davies, Michael Holmes, and George Davey Smith wrote a guide to Mendelian randomization for clinicians in 2018. The method uses genetic differences as a natural experiment. It tests whether a changeable risk factor truly causes a health outcome.

The guide explains the logic in plain terms, with a glossary and a checklist for reading such studies. It stresses the assumptions that must hold and the ways results can mislead. Clinicians meet these studies in journals more and more often. The checklist helps them judge whether a claimed cause deserves to change practice or needs more proof first.
pmc-6191528:
Ray Dorsey, Alexis Elbaz, Emma Nichols, and Global Burden of Disease colleagues tracked Parkinson disease worldwide in 2018. Nerve disorders are now the top source of disability across the globe. Aging populations push diseases like Parkinson disease upward each year.

The study measures cases, deaths, and disability for most countries from 1990 to 2016. The number of people living with Parkinson disease more than doubled over that span. Growth was fastest where populations aged fastest, not only where care improved. Planners use these trends to argue for more specialists, drugs, and carer support.
pmc-6377728:
Yuan Zhang, Ying Liu, Haiying Liu, and coauthors reviewed exosomes and their clinical promise in 2019. Exosomes are nano-sized bubbles released when internal cell compartments fuse with the cell surface. They travel in blood and other body fluids.

Each exosome carries proteins, lipids, and genetic material stamped by its parent cell. Neighboring and distant cells can take them up and change behavior. That courier role makes exosomes attractive as disease markers and as drug carriers. The review weighs strong early results against hard problems in purity, dosing, and large-scale production.
pmc-6436528:
Robert Bowers, Nikos Kyrpides, Ramunas Stepanauskas, and a large group proposed genome reporting standards in 2017. Most microbes cannot be grown in culture. Their genomes come from single cells or from mixed community samples instead.

The MISAG and MIMAG standards set what must be reported with such genomes. They grade genomes by completeness and contamination and ask for basic facts like size and gene counts. Shared grades let databases and readers judge quality at a glance. The standards brought order to a flood of uncultivated genomes entering public archives. Journals and databases were urged to ask authors for these data with every genome submission.
pmc-6859528:
Sai Srinivas Upadhyayula, Bryce Tan, Balamurugan Vellayappan, and coauthors reviewed reactive oxygen and DNA damage in cancer in 2019. Reactive oxygen species are short-lived molecules that can break DNA. Cells answer with a damage response that pauses growth and orders repair.

Evidence from labs and clinics ties this interplay to how chemotherapy and radiation work. Tumors often live with high damage and lean hard on repair paths. Blocking repair can then kill cancer cells selectively. The review maps that logic and the drugs now testing it in patients. Early-phase trials combining repair blockers with radiation are described in detail.
pmc-7410828:
The ENCODE Project Consortium, with Jill Moore and colleagues among the lead authors, reported in 2020 a greatly widened map of the working parts of the human and mouse genomes. Genes that spell out proteins are only a small share of the genome. The rest holds switches and signals that govern when each gene turns on, in which cells, and by how much.

In this third phase of the long running project, the team expanded its catalog of these control elements using many assay types across many cell types. The result is a shared reference that other scientists query daily when they study how a genetic change might affect health. It turns raw genome letters into a labeled map of function.
pmc-7778928:
Matty Blum and co-authors marked twenty years of the InterPro database in 2020. InterPro sorts protein sequences into families and flags the domains and conserved sites that hint at a protein's function. It does this by combining the classification schemes of many member databases into one searchable whole.

The article recounts how the resource grew over two decades and describes the software, InterProScan, that applies its classifications to new sequences, including DNA and RNA derived ones. It also looks at how the database is maintained and used today. Anyone who has pasted a protein sequence into a website and received a family name has likely used the machinery this history describes.
pmc-8007028:
Matthew Page and co-authors presented PRISMA 2020 in 2021, a refreshed reporting guideline that reviewers of combined studies are asked to follow. Systematic reviews gather every study on a question and combine the results, so their value depends on readers being able to see exactly how the work was done. The new guideline replaces the widely used 2009 version.

The authors describe what changed and why, including fuller reporting of searches, of how studies were selected, and of how certain the combined evidence is. The statement is short by design, a checklist meant to sit beside a manuscript as it is written. Because journals across medicine endorse it, this brief document shapes evidence reporting far beyond its own pages.
pmc-8063428:
Sonam Gurung and co-authors traced in 2021 the full life story of exosomes, tiny bubble-like packages that cells release and other cells take up. Exosomes are a class of small extracellular vesicles, and they carry proteins and genetic material between cells as a form of messaging. Clinical trials testing them for diagnosis and therapy have drawn strong interest from scientists and investors alike.

The authors follow exosomes from their formation inside a cell, through their release and travel, to their uptake and the signals they deliver at the destination. They also review what makes loading and targeting them so tricky in practice. The account gives readers the biology behind a technology often hyped ahead of the evidence.
pmc-8677728:
Yan He and co-authors reviewed in 2021 efforts to treat cancer by targeting the PI3K/Akt signaling pathway. This pathway helps govern cell growth, survival, and metabolism, and it is switched on abnormally in many cancers, helping tumors arise and progress. Because it has many connected nodes, examining the signals above and below it can reveal the full picture of its influence.

The review maps those upstream triggers and downstream effects, then surveys drugs aimed at different points along the route. It weighs the successes and the side effects that have limited this class of medicines so far. For drug developers, the pathway remains one of the richest and most frustrating targets in oncology.
podcast-joerogan-7-IOCUCDL28:
Episode 377 of the Joe Rogan Experience catches Duncan Trussell in the show's early, wild years. Trussell, a comedian with a mystic streak, was already a core member of Rogan's circle. The young show had fewer rules then, and this visit shows it.

The talk jumps between psychedelic stories, jokes about the self, and sudden deep turns on love and death. Trussell's free, riffing style fills the room, and Rogan matches his energy. Listeners who know Trussell's later, calmer work will hear the rawer version here, a snapshot of podcasting before the format grew polished.
podcast-tuckercarlson-qk3I6xi7c28:
Tucker Carlson sits with Donald Trump and asks him flat out what truly happened to Jeffrey Epstein. The episode title is built on that one exchange. Carlson puts the question that hangs over the whole case.

Trump gives his answer on the death and the files in his own words. Carlson presses on what the public still does not know. The clip of the clash is the heart of the episode. Listeners can hear the exchange whole, not cut into bits by the press. The library keeps the talk as a record of that rare, blunt moment.
poems-1828:
Thomas Gent collected his Poems for a London edition of 1828, gathering pieces that had appeared separately over the years and adding many printed for the first time. His advertisement thanks the critics who reviewed the earlier verses kindly, judging them by their pretensions as the amusement of a working man's leisure hours. Gent wrote as someone whose fortune would not let him devote his life to poetry.

The preface turns personal at the end, where Gent records a heavy domestic bereavement suffered while the book was in the press. Praises the lost family member for her love of literature and science, shown in her lectures on the physiology of the senses. That grief shadows the volume. Readers meet a humble, earnest versifier of the 1820s, and a book shaped as much by a working life as by literary ambition.
poems-pg10328:
Walter R. Cassels published his Poems in London in 1856, a single volume by a Victorian writer better known later for theological controversy than for verse. The contents open with two longer pieces, Mabel and Hebe. Then move into the short lyrics and sonnets of a young man's book: Spring, the Bittern, Gone, a serenade, and the Eagle. Cassels writes in the mid-century manner, polished, melancholy, and fond of classical names.

Sonnet sequences mark public and private griefs, including sonnets on the death of the Duke of Wellington. Pieces such as the Dark River, the Delectable Mountains, and Under the Sea reach for allegory. A withered rose-bud, a shell, and a raven supply the era's favorite emblems. The volume is a fair specimen of the respectable poetry Victorians produced in quantity and posterity mostly forgot, worth reading as a record of its moment's taste.
procopius-wars-gothic-3-dewing-1928:
The History of the Wars of Procopius ends with books seven and eight, in H. B. Dewing's Loeb volume of 1928. Totila's Goths still hold Italy, and Justinian sends the eunuch general Narses with a great army to finish the war. Procopius brings his vast work to its close.

Narses crushes Totila at Taginae and ends the Gothic kingdom at Mons Lactarius. The last book sweeps wider, to Persia, the Danube, and the Slavs pressing the frontier. Italy lies saved and ruined at once, its cities emptied by twenty years of war. Procopius is the chief witness of the whole reconquest. His final books ask what the victory was worth.
punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-158-19:
Punch for January 28, 1920, opens as usual with Charivaria, a string of brief comic notes on the news of the week. The London weekly was in its 158th volume, amusing readers who were facing high prices and short supplies in peacetime Britain.

Petrol rising eightpence a gallon leads the column, with the warning that walkers must settle for being knocked down by horses. Moleskins at eighteen pence, a motor-coat at three hundred pounds lined with Persian lamb, and coal steamers returning from Calais with champagne all get a twist. A Walworth girl with a mania for Tube travel closes the list.
punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-159-19:
Volume 159 of Punch opens its July 28, 1920, number with Charivaria, the weekly column of short jokes drawn from the papers. Railways, wages, and foreign affairs give the column its usual mixed bag.

The public, says one paper, will not stand for higher rail fares, having stood too much at the old ones. A Mile End duck laid four eggs in one day. Tube trains now run from the Bank to Ealing in thirty-five minutes, and Mersey shipyard men demand higher pay for not working than for working. Petrograd's search for a public executioner is offered as a steady job for someone.
raphael-manual-of-astrology-1828:
Raphael was the pen name of Robert Cross Smith, a London astrologer whose Manual of Astrology, or Book of the Stars, appeared in 1828. Astrology had sunk to almanac level in England, and Raphael set out to raise it. His manual became the founding text of the nineteenth-century astrological revival.

He teaches chart casting, nativities, and the judgment of daily questions in a brisk, popular style meant for self-taught readers. His almanacs and guides sold the art back to a Regency public that had nearly forgotten it. Every later English astrological writer worked in a market Raphael reopened.
russell-sceptical-essays-1928:
Sceptical Essays, published in 1928, collects Russell's shorter pieces applying rational doubt to religion, morals, politics, and everyday belief. His prescription is in the first essay: when the experts disagree, the non-expert does well to doubt.

Essay by essay he examines free thought, the dangers of propaganda, and the harm done by good intentions armed with power. Russell writes as a public teacher, witty and exact, refusing every comfortable fog. The targets change with the years, but the method never dates. These essays show the most famous skeptic of the century at his most readable and most humane.
schleiermacher-christian-faith-1928:
The Christian Faith, in the translation by H R Mackintosh and J S Stewart of 1928, is Friedrich Schleiermacher's Der christliche Glaube of 1821 to 1822. The English version is complete, and it carries the magnum opus of liberal Protestant theology. Schleiermacher spent a life preaching and teaching at Berlin, and this book gathers his whole system of doctrine.

His key phrase is the feeling of absolute dependence, the heart's sense of resting wholly on God. Every doctrine, from creation to the church to last things, is traced to that feeling in the believer's life. Critics call the system vast, subtle, and hard to storm. It still anchors the study of modern theology.
senior-two-lectures-population-1828:
Senior's Two Lectures on Population, delivered at Oxford in 1828, give his answer to Malthus on the great question of the age. Malthus had taught that population grows faster than food, so misery must check the numbers. Senior grants the race between mouths and loaves but disputes the finish.

He adds the check Malthus slighted: prudence. As people grow more decent in their wants, Senior argues, they delay marriage and limit families to protect their standard of life. The desire for improvement can thus outrun the pressure of numbers. The lectures soften the gloomy science with common sense and were praised for their humanity. They include his exchange with Malthus himself, who answered in letters printed with the lectures. The old classical school appears here at its most humane.
smith-rabia-the-mystic-1928:
Margaret Smith wrote the first Western study of Rabi'a al-Adawiyya, the slave girl of Basra who became the first great woman saint of Islam. Her book appeared from Cambridge in 1928. Rabi'a died in 801, famed for a love of God that asked no heaven and feared no hell.

Smith gathers the tales and sayings of Rabi'a from the Arabic sources and sets her among her fellow saints. She treats the women of early Islam and the growth of Sufi teaching on divine love. Rabi'a's lamp, her donkey, and her blunt prayers come alive in the telling. The book founded the study of women in Sufism in the West.
spence-mysteries-britain-1928:
Lewis Spence, a Scots writer on myth and folk lore, wrote this survey of the hidden rites of Britain in 1928. He had spent years on the myths of many lands. Here he turned to the isle he knew best and its deep past.

Spence walked from the druids to the great stone rings and the lore of old shrines. He held that a native rite line ran through British life from the far past. Some claims go past the proof, but the book sums up his case in one place.
spengler-decline-west-vol-2-1928:
Oswald Spengler's The Decline of the West, Volume 2, appears in Atkinson's translation of 1928. Subtitled Perspectives of World-History, the volume completes Spengler's work. He turns to the state, money, and the destiny of peoples. Democracy, in his account, yields to money power and then to Caesarism, rule by strong men.

Spengler surveys cities, classes, and religions across his eight great cultures. The West's final phase, he predicts, will be an age of empire and engineering without new art. Many reject his fatalism; few ignore his sweep. The two volumes form a vast, gloomy system. They remain essential for the study of historical pessimism between the wars.
spr-proceedings-vol36-1926-1928:
Volume thirty six gathers parts ninety seven through one hundred three, spanning 1926 to 1928. Seven parts in one binding close the run of Proceedings held here. The Society for Psychical Research had published since 1882, testing wonders by committee rule. Telepathy, apparitions, and trance mediumship fill these last parts as they filled the first.

Sittings, surveys, and spontaneous cases stand reported with the old care. The archive these volumes build is the primary record of the evidential debate to 1930. No verdict ends it; the files simply stand open. Volume thirty six completes the set on this shelf. Readers can now cross the whole span in order.
state-of-the-union-addresses-pg5028:
Chester A. Arthur gives four yearly addresses, from December 6, 1881, to December 1, 1884, parted by three stars. The first opens on a dread blow. Since the people's chosen house last met, a shocking loss has fallen on the nation, and but for it the year could be recalled with pure content. Harvests were plenteous, crafts of all kinds thrived, health held, and peace with foreign governments stood unbroken.

To the hid will that took the loved and famed citizen who was lately head of the nation, Arthur bows in sorrow. The dead man's high character, noble deeds, and patriotic life will be kept, he says, as a sacred store of the whole people. Word of his death drew marks of grief from foreign governments and folk, proofs of the kinship of nations that the past will record with care.
summers-vampire-kith-kin-1928:
Montague Summers gave the vampire its first full study in 1928. The Vampire: His Kith and Kin draws on lore from all over the world. Summers was a priest who took the old tales in full earnest. He treats the vampire as a true foe of man and God.

Tales from Greece, Slav lands, and the far East fill the book. He sorts the kinds of the undead and tells how men fought them. Church law, trial tales, and folk rites all get a place. The book set the base for all grave study of the vampire since.
the-great-round-world-and-what-is-going-: The issue of May 20, 1897 is No. 28 of The Great Round World and What Is Going On in It, a weekly newspaper for boys and girls. Only front matter is present here. It gives the masthead and a special inducement. The same atlas offer stands here as in the two numbers before it. A subscriber who sends $2.50 for a year's subscription to a new name gets Rand, McNally and Company's 1897 Atlas of the World. The atlas has 160 pages of colored maps from new plates.
the-history-of-don-quixote-volume-2-part:
Volume 2, Part 28 of Don Quixote comes from Cervantes, in Ormsby's English rendering. Chapter twenty-nine tells of the famous adventure of the enchanted bark. Two days after leaving the grove, Don Quixote and Sancho reach the river Ebro, and the sight gives the knight great delight.

He gazes on the charm of the banks, the clearness of the stream, the gentle current, and the wealth of crystal waters. The pleasant view stirs a thousand tender thoughts, above all his memories of the cave of Montesinos. Calm water and fond musing set the stage for a boat that the knight will read as enchantment.
the-mirror-of-literature-amusement-and-i:
The great Druidical temple at Abury in Wiltshire fills the Mirror's No. 341, dated Saturday, November 15, 1828. Lines from Shakespeare, 'sermons in stones,' head the piece. The engraving shows the temple's original state before modern vandalism levelled much of its grandeur. A grand circle contained two minor circles, the outer ring covering upwards of twenty-eight acres within a ditch.

Dr. Stukeley's reckoning lists the parts: an outward circle of one hundred stones, northern and southern temples, a cove of three stones, a central obelisk, and a ring stone. Two avenues of two hundred stones each approached the site on a gradual ascent. The whole form, the article says, was a snake, symbol of eternity, its head carried up Hackpen Hill. Readers get Avebury restored on paper to a serpent of standing stones.
the-project-gutenberg-encyclopedia-volum:
Volume 1 of the Project Gutenberg Encyclopedia reproduces a 1911 edition whose original title and publisher go unnamed. Notices explain that the publisher's trademark licence was refused as inconsistent with the project's volunteer, noncommercial aims, so the preface was omitted. Readers are warned that the information is old and reflects the outlook of a century ago. The volume, once also called Encyclopedia Anglicana, spans twenty-eight volumes plus an index.

The first article treats the letter A. It corresponds, the entry says, to the first symbol of the Phoenician alphabet and almost all its descendants. In Phoenician, a represented not a vowel but a breathing, as did the symbols for e and o. The vowels originally went unmarked by those signs. The entry begins the alphabet's run through the volume.
thompson-epic-of-gilgamish-1928:
R. Campbell Thompson published The Epic of Gilgamish at Oxford's Clarendon Press in 1928. He spells the hero Gilgamish throughout, following his reading of the tablets. Thompson, a British Museum Assyriologist, made his verse translation from a fresh collation of the cuneiform tablets in London.

Gilgamesh, king of Uruk, loses his friend Enkidu and journeys past death's waters seeking eternal life. He returns with a story, a plant lost to a snake, and hard wisdom about fame. Thompson renders the epic in English hexameters meant to echo its stride. His version was the standard interwar English Gilgamesh. Readers met in it the oldest epic hero whose tale survives.
tob-10228:
James Legge's translation presents the Tao Teh King in eighty-one brief chapters under the name Lao Tzu. Legge was a pioneering Victorian translator of Chinese classics. The verses urge rulers and readers alike to govern by not forcing things against their nature.

Yield like water, desire little, and let people and events follow their own course: that counsel repeats in cryptic, compressed lines. Chinese thought on power and humility has drawn on these chapters for two millennia. English readers of Legge's version meet the text in formal Victorian dress, which can feel distant, yet the paradoxes still cut against ambition and control.
tob-10628:
Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri, a blind Syrian poet who died over a thousand years ago, filled his Diwan with rhymed meditations on fate and folly. He was a skeptic in a religious age. His verses distrust clerics, pity the credulous, and urge doing no harm to any living thing; he himself lived as a strict vegetarian.

Poems in the collection turn over death, hypocrisy, ambition, and the vanity of sects that kill over doctrine. The voice is bleak and brilliant at once, funny in its contempt and tender toward animals and outcasts. English readers meet a freethinker from the medieval Arab world who sounds startlingly modern.
tob-10828:
Annie Besant edited the posthumous third volume of The Secret Doctrine from H. P. Blavatsky's remaining papers. Its subjects shift from cosmic theory toward occult practice and esoteric history. Because Blavatsky did not live to shape it, the volume is more fragmentary than the first two books of the set.

Loose papers on hidden teachings, initiates, and disputed points of doctrine read like notes from a workshop rather than a finished system. Scholars debate how much reflects Blavatsky's final intentions. V1 evidence directs the volume to committed students of Theosophy rather than beginners; newcomers should start with her Key to Theosophy and return here for depth.
tob-13328:
Valmiki, the sage poet of ancient India, composed the Ramayana, one of the two great Sanskrit epics. R. T. H. Griffith turned it into English verse in the nineteenth century. The epic holds a central place in Hindu life and art across Asia.

Prince Rama is exiled to the forest with his wife Sita and his brother Lakshmana. When the demon king Ravana steals Sita away to Lanka, Rama allies with the monkey host and wages war to win her back. The seven books join high adventure to dharma, the law of duty that Rama's life displays in full.
tob-4028:
Immanuel Kant published the Critique of Pure Reason in 1781, asking what reason can and cannot know. His answer reshaped philosophy: we know things as they appear to us, never things in themselves, because space, time, and causality are forms our own mind imposes on experience. Kant called the shift his Copernican revolution in thought.

God, freedom, and immortality fall outside theoretical proof, though they return as needs of moral life. The prose is formidable, architected like a cathedral, and readers should expect slow going. Two centuries of argument later, the Critique remains the mountain modern philosophy is still climbing or deliberately circling.
tob-4128:
Mead's 1896 Pistis Sophia, translated from the Coptic, gave modern readers their first full Gnostic gospel. The risen Savior teaches his disciples for years after the resurrection, the text claims, and at its heart stands Pistis Sophia, Faith-Wisdom, a fallen power who repents through the aeons.

Her thirteen repentances, sung as psalms, plead for rescue from the rulers of darkness. Jesus answers with readings of psalms and odes as coded accounts of her fall. The cosmology is vast and strange. Verified from the 1919 edition, Mead's version introduced Gnosticism to the modern world and still opens the subject.
tob-9028:
Augustine of Hippo wrote The City of God across the years after Rome's sack in 410, and Marcus Dods's translation presents volume one here. Pagans charged that Christians had caused the disaster by abandoning the old gods. Augustine answers that Rome's gods failed long before Christ, and that Rome's own vices, celebrated by its historians, rotted it from within.

From that defense grows his larger vision of two cities, earthly and divine, contending through history toward judgment. The first volume handles Rome's religion and early calamities in detail. Few books have taught the West to think historically as this one did; volume one lays the foundation stone by stone.
troilus-and-cressida-pg1528: A scene-by-scene contents list is all that opens this second Troilus and Cressida record, credited to William Shakespeare. Act one moves from Priam's palace to a Troy street, then to the Grecian camp before Agamemnon's tent. Act three brings Pandarus's orchard and the Greek camp. Act four tours Troy streets and houses, and act five returns to the camps of Achilles and Calchas. Only the contents are present here, so the play itself does not appear. The companion record in this set carries the folio-style text.
un-ga-res-28:
Ruined towns and dead farms fill the opening of Resolution 28, passed by the General Assembly on 2 February 1946. The war of aggression, it says, had smashed vast areas of member states on a scale never seen. The hurt lands held near half the people of the world. Their loss cut world trade, drove living standards down, and in some places wiped out normal work and trade in full.

To make good the ruin, the text argues, vast sums of new capital goods must flow into the smashed areas. Left alone, most states could not rebuild at the speed the task demands. The vote set out the case for the great aid flows that soon reshaped the postwar world.
un-ga-res-a-69-28:
New tools of talk and trade can serve peace or harm it, and Resolution A/69/28, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session, weighs that edge. The vote stands in a chain that goes back to 1998, on the role of science and skill in world safety. States had long agreed that the fruits of science have two faces: they can serve plain, civil ends, or be bent to war.

Great strides in data tools and long-range talk are noted with care. In that growth, the Assembly sees the widest chance for good: for the spread of wealth, health, and free ties between peoples. The task it sets is to guard the civil path of such tools, while curbing their use as arms.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
General Assembly Resolution 28, adopted on 2 February 1946, named the rebuilding of war-wrecked member countries a grave and pressing task. The Assembly noted that lands holding near half the world's people had suffered damage on a scale never seen before. Living standards, health, and output were badly cut. World trade was thrown off course.

Full rebuilding, the text held, would take vast sums of new plant and goods. The hurt countries could not supply them alone. The Assembly set the matter for deep study by its Second Committee. That was for the second part of the first session. It asked the Economic and Social Council to take it up at once as well.

Resolution 69/28 of the General Assembly deals with information and telecommunications in international security — in current terms, state behavior in cyberspace. The Assembly notes both the gains of new information technologies and the danger in them. They may be used against states' infrastructure, or for criminal and terrorist ends. It welcomes the work of its Group of Governmental Experts on norms of responsible state behavior and confidence-building. It tells the group to continue studying threats and how international law applies. It invites member states to keep submitting their views.
un-sc-res-1028: Acting formally, the Security Council produced the decision numbered 1028, catalogued under 1995. Such texts can call for cease-fires, set up missions, impose duties, or settle points of UN procedure and membership. Its value lies in the primary wording: the decision as adopted, kept through the Wikisource transcription of the record. No summary replaces it; the record itself is the content of the entry.
un-sc-res-128:
Lebanon charged in 1958 that the United Arab Republic was interfering in its internal affairs. Resolution 128, adopted on 11 June 1958, came after the Council heard Lebanon's charges and the reply of the United Arab Republic. The vote was ten to none, with the Soviet Union abstaining, though the heading also calls the vote unanimous.

The Council decides to send an observation group to Lebanon at once. Its job is to make sure there is no illegal movement of people, arms, or other supplies across the Lebanese borders. The Secretary-General is given power to take the steps needed to send the group, and the group must keep the Council informed through him.
un-sc-res-1328:
UNDOF's six-month rhythm on the Golan Heights rolled on in late 2000. On 27 November 2000 the Security Council renewed the force until 31 May 2001. The Secretary-General had reported on it ten days earlier. The Council also restated its standards for the health of peacekeepers. The mission's terms stayed exactly as before.

The parties had to carry out resolution 338 without delay. The Secretary-General owed a closing report on the term. It would track events and measures taken toward 338. UNDOF's observers manned the line drawn after the 1973 war. Their quiet patrols had become a fixture of the Israel-Syria frontier.
un-sc-res-1428:
UNIFIL's mandate in southern Lebanon came up again in July 2002. On 30 July 2002 the Security Council extended the force for six months. The new term ran until 31 January 2003. The Secretary-General had recommended the renewal in his July report. He was also reshaping the force to match conditions on the ground. The Council backed that reconfiguration work.

The text recalls that Israel had withdrawn in line with resolution 425. Lebanon's return of authority to the south remained a goal. The Council restated Lebanon's sovereignty and territorial integrity. It also repeated the call for calm along the withdrawal line. The force's size was being trimmed as its tasks shifted to observation.
un-sc-res-1528:
Côte d'Ivoire is the subject of United Nations Security Council Resolution 1528, adopted on 27 February 2004. The Forces Nouvelles had returned to the unity government under the Linas-Marcoussis deal. Talks on disarmament had begun. The country's economy was sinking, with harm across the region. The president and West African states both asked for a full peacekeeping operation.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council creates the United Nations Operation in Côte d'Ivoire, UNOCI, for twelve months from 4 April 2004. Up to 6,240 troops and 350 civilian police will watch the cease-fire and guard disarmament sites. The mission will protect civilians, back elections planned for 2005, and help restore state authority. French forces keep their supporting role for the same year.
un-sc-res-1628:
The Congo mission received a one-month extension in September 2005. On 30 September 2005 the Security Council kept MONUC until 31 October 2005. The mandate stayed as set by four earlier resolutions. All of them had been adopted under Chapter VII. The Council restated the Congo's sovereignty and borders. It also restated its readiness to back the peace process. The country was then preparing its first free elections in decades.

The short term bridged a planning gap. A larger mandate with election support was being drafted. The Council stayed actively seized of the matter. MONUC was already one of the largest peace operations in the world. Its final shape for the election period came with the next renewal.
un-sc-res-1728:
Cyprus again comes before the Council in United Nations Security Council Resolution 1728. The Council adopted it on 15 December 2006. The Green Line stayed calm, and mine clearing in the buffer zone was moving ahead. Yet trust between the two communities stayed low, and an 8 July deal had stalled.

The text extends the United Nations Peacekeeping Force in Cyprus, called UNFICYP, until 15 June 2007. It presses both sides to carry out the July deal and finish groundwork for full talks. It calls on the Turkish Cypriot side to restore the old military position at Strovilia. The Secretary-General had to report back by 1 June 2007.
un-sc-res-1828:
Action on Darfur came with Resolution 1828, adopted on 31 July 2008. One year into the joint African Union and United Nations mission, UNAMID, safety in Darfur had grown worse. Attacks on civilians and aid workers went on. The World Court prosecutor had just asked for an arrest warrant for Sudan's president.

The text extends the mandate of UNAMID for twelve months, to 31 July 2009. It urges a fast build-up, with eighty per cent of the force in place by the end of 2008. Sudan must drop all blocks on the mission's movement and work. All sides are told to stop attacks and agree to a firm, lasting cease-fire.
un-sc-res-1928:
North Korea's nuclear and missile programs kept a sanctions panel at work in 2010. On 7 June 2010 the Security Council extended that panel for a year. The Panel of Experts helps enforce the sanctions set after North Korea's nuclear tests. Its mandate now ran until 12 June 2011. The panel had sent an interim report in 2009 and a final one in May 2010.

The panel owed a midterm report by 12 November 2010. A final report would come before the mandate ended. The Council urged all states and United Nations bodies to cooperate with it. Sharing facts on sanctions breaches mattered most. The text treats weapons proliferation as a standing threat to peace.
un-sc-res-228:
A large Israeli raid into Jordan drew censure from the Security Council on 25 November 1966. The attack had struck the southern Hebron area on 13 November 1966. The Secretary-General's statement of 16 November and report of 18 November laid out the facts. The Council found a large-scale, carefully planned military action on Jordanian territory by Israel's armed forces.

The Council deplored the loss of life and the heavy damage to property. It censured Israel for the action, which broke the United Nations Charter and the Israel-Jordan General Armistice Agreement. Israel was told plainly that military reprisals cannot be tolerated. If they were repeated, the Council would have to weigh further and more effective steps under the Charter to stop them. The Secretary-General was asked to keep watch on the situation and report as needed. The raid, on the village of Samu, was the largest Israeli operation since 1956.
un-sc-res-2728:
Gaza occupied the Council on 25 March 2024, when it adopted Resolution 2728 on Gaza. Months of war had left the Gaza Strip in a catastrophic state. Civilians lacked food, water, and medical care at any real scale. Egypt, Qatar, and the United States were pressing for a halt to the fighting and freedom for hostages.

The Council demands an immediate ceasefire for the month of Ramadan, respected by all parties. That pause should lead to a lasting, sustainable ceasefire. All hostages must be freed at once and without conditions. Barriers to aid at scale must come down across the whole Strip. The text also recalls that taking hostages breaks international law.
un-sc-res-28: Members of the Council adopted Resolution 28 on Greece on 6 August 1947 by ten votes to none, with one abstention. Rival drafts on the Greek question had left the Council stuck. The Council sets up a small sub-committee for the job. It is made of the delegations that had put forward proposals or changes. Their task is to test whether a fresh draft can win broad support. The sub-committee must report its findings on 11 August 1947. The text does nothing else.
un-sc-res-328:
Southern Rhodesia's raids on Zambia drew a broad rebuke on 10 March 1973. A special mission sent under resolution 326 (1973) had reported on the border crisis. South Africa refused to pull its military and armed forces out of Southern Rhodesia, defying resolutions 277 (1970) and 326 (1973). Britain, as the administering power, held the main duty to end the illegal minority regime.

The Council backed the mission's findings in full. Rhodesia's recent acts of provocation and aggression against Zambia had raised the tension, it declared. The only real answer lay in the people of Zimbabwe winning self-determination and independence. South Africa was strongly condemned for keeping its forces in place, and the demand for their instant withdrawal was repeated. The Rhodesia sanctions committee was told to speed its work. The Council urged Britain to call a national constitutional conference at once, so majority rule could follow.
un-sc-res-428: Council action recorded as Resolution 428 appears in this catalog under the year 1976. Formal decisions of this sort guide UN staff, peacekeeping forces, and governments in the years that follow. What is preserved is the exact formal wording, transcribed on English Wikisource from the official record of the Council. Its place here reflects the library's aim of keeping primary records readable.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci: Security Council resolution 1028, adopted unanimously on 8 December 1995, briefly extends the mandate of UNAMIR, the United Nations Assistance Mission for Rwanda. The Council had considered the Secretary-General's report of 1 December 1995 on the mission. It extends the mandate only until 12 December 1995. That is a four-day bridge while it decides the mission's future. It decides to remain actively seized of the situation in Rwanda.

Security Council resolution 128, adopted on 11 June 1958, answers Lebanon's charge that the United Arab Republic was interfering in its internal affairs. The Council had heard both sides. It decides to send an observation group to Lebanon urgently. The group is to make sure there is no illegal infiltration of men or supply of arms or other material across the Lebanese borders. The Council authorizes the Secretary-General to take the steps needed. It asks the group to keep it informed through him.

Some summaries file Resolution 1328 under Western Sahara, but the text concerns the Golan Heights. It passed unanimously on 27 November 2000. Members had just reviewed the Secretary-General's report of 17 November. The subject was the UN Disengagement Observer Force. That force monitors the separation zone between Israeli and Syrian troops.

The mandate was extended by six months, to 31 May 2001. The Council again urged both parties to put Resolution 338 of 1973 into effect. That older resolution links the observer mission to a negotiated Middle East peace. A further report from the Secretary-General was requested for the end of the period.

Half a year more for the Lebanon watch came in the summer of 2002. Beirut asked for it in a note dated 9 July. The chief's report of 12 July backed the plea. He also set out a leaner shape for the force. Resolution 1428 passed with no dissent on 30 July 2002.

UNIFIL's term ran to 31 January 2003. The chief had to press on with the reshape. Troop states and Beirut would be brought into the talks. Lebanon won praise for steps to rule its south once more. Its army's spread there was cheered. All sides had to honor the Blue Line in full. Acts of force drew blame. Breaches by air, sea, and land were called grave. Praise flowed for the force's mine work and for a new aid group backing it.

Côte d'Ivoire gets a UN peacekeeping operation in Resolution 1528, adopted unanimously on 27 February 2004. The Linas-Marcoussis Agreement had set a peace path, the Forces Nouvelles had rejoined the government, and a disarmament programme was agreed. Côte d'Ivoire's president and ECOWAS had both asked the Council to turn the small MINUCI mission into a full operation.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council establishes the United Nations Operation in Côte d'Ivoire, UNOCI, for 12 months from 4 April 2004, with up to 6,240 military personnel and 350 civilian police. UNOCI must monitor the ceasefire, support disarmament and demobilization, guard surrendered weapons, protect civilians under imminent threat, help restore state authority and policing, and assist preparations for the 2005 presidential election. It may use all necessary means. French forces are authorized for the same period to support UNOCI and protect civilians in their areas.

Resolution 1628, adopted on 30 September 2005, keeps a large peacekeeping mission in place for one more month. The mission is MONUC, deployed in the Democratic Republic of the Congo during the country's fragile move from civil war toward elections. The Council restated its respect for Congo's sovereignty and its support for peace and national reconciliation.

The single decision extends MONUC's mandate, set out in several earlier resolutions and backed by Chapter VII authority, until 31 October 2005. A one-month rollover of this kind usually signals that a bigger decision on the mission's size and tasks is still being negotiated. The Council closed by keeping the Congo question formally on its agenda.

Cyprus stays calm but divided in Resolution 1728, adopted on 15 December 2006. An 8 July agreement had set out shared ground: the present state of affairs was not acceptable, and a bicommunal, bizonal federation with political equality was the goal. Lack of trust had blocked every step since. Mine clearing in the buffer zone was moving ahead, and the zone might be mine-free within two years.

The Council gives full support to the UN Peacekeeping Force in Cyprus, UNFICYP, and extends its mandate until 15 June 2007.
